examples.name: labeled-buttons
examples.title: Labelled icon buttons
examples.summary: A toolbar of three icon-only buttons (Play, Add, Search), each carrying a contentDescription and marked clickable for screen readers; DX-04 is the same toolbar without them.
examples.prompt: Make a toolbar of icon-only buttons (play, add, search) that a screen reader can announce.
teaches: Label an icon-only button with semantics contentDescription so a screen reader can announce it
Mark it as an actionable element with semantics clickable: true (the JSON has no role key; Java and json2rc write role 255, unset)
Highlight the last-pressed button with conditionalOperations eq @selected i inside each button's canvas

snippets.note: semantics: contentDescription "Play", clickable
onClick: selected = 0
the accent background when this button was the last pressed

check.describe: inspect_accessibility lists three clickable nodes labelled Play, Add and Search, and the audit has no a11y finding. A tap on Search turns its circle blue. Resized (240, 540 wide) the three 56 dp buttons stay evenly spread across the width; the tap on Search (moved to its new centre) still turns it blue.

pitfalls: semantics has no role key in the Java parser (it reads contentDescription, text, stateDescription, enabled and clickable); a "role" is silently dropped, so use clickable: true to mark a button
semantics clickable: true only tells the screen reader the node is actionable; the onClick modifier on the same component is what makes it act
Name the action ("Search"), not the picture ("magnifying glass"); an icon-only button has no text for a screen reader to fall back on

examples.name: state-description
examples.title: Switch that announces its state
examples.summary: A Bluetooth switch whose semantics carry a stateDescription, so a screen reader says "Bluetooth, Off" or "Bluetooth, On".
examples.prompt: Make an on/off switch for Bluetooth that a screen reader announces as "On" or "Off".
teaches: Announce a control's state with semantics stateDescription next to its contentDescription
Give each state its own component with a fixed stateDescription and swap them with visibility, since stateDescription takes a text, not an expression
Flip the two visibility integers from one onClick with two valueIntegerChange actions

snippets.note: semantics: contentDescription Bluetooth, stateDescription Off, clickable
the On variant
onClick: showOn = 1, showOff = 0

check.describe: inspect_accessibility shows the switch labelled Bluetooth with state Off (and the hidden On variant); a tap shows the teal On switch. Resized (240, 540 wide) the label takes the remaining width and the switch stays at the end; tapped at its new position it turns On.

pitfalls: stateDescription is resolved to a text id when the document is written; it cannot follow a float, so build one component per state and swap them with visibility
visibility reads an integer variable: declare it with "vtype": "int" and flip it with valueIntegerChange; each onClick must set both integers
Accessibility inspectors also list the component that visibility currently hides (the inspector does not yet drop GONE components)
Visibility changes cross-fade (about half a second in the C++ player); render a little after the tap to see the settled state

examples.name: document-description
examples.title: Chart with a document description
examples.summary: A drawn bar chart of weekly steps whose header contentDescription summarises it for screen readers, since the bars themselves carry no text.
examples.prompt: Draw a weekly steps bar chart and give it a spoken summary for screen readers.
teaches: Summarise a drawn-only document for screen readers with header.contentDescription
Describe what the chart says (start, peak, end, with numbers), not what it looks like

snippets.note: the whole document's spoken summary
one bar

check.describe: Seven blue bars (3k, 5k, 4k, 7k, 6k, 9k, 8k) peaking on Saturday; validate's header shows the contentDescription (DOC_CONTENT_DESCRIPTION tag). Resized (240×180, 540×120) the bars are scaled to the canvas (one scale by componentWidth()/360, componentHeight()/180) and the day letters follow their centres.

pitfalls: At apiLevel 7 the description is only a header tag (DOC_CONTENT_DESCRIPTION); the RootContentDescription operation is written only for apiLevel 6 with profiles 0, so a player or tool that reads only that operation sees no description
Keep the description in step with the data: a canvas has no text a screen reader could read instead, so a stale or vague summary is all the user gets

A chart drawn in literal coordinates (bars at x 30…322, a 360×180 background rect) sits in the top-left corner of a larger host and is cut in a smaller one: paint the background with a modifier and scale or derive the geometry from componentWidth() / componentHeight()

examples.name: touch-targets
examples.title: 48 dp touch targets
examples.summary: Three 20 dp icons (Close, More options, Info) each centred in an invisible 48×48 dp clickable box, and a 48 dp tall Send button.
examples.prompt: Make a row of small icon buttons (close, more, info) and a Send button whose tap areas are at least 48 dp.
teaches: Keep the hit area at least 48×48 dp: put onClick on a size 48 box and draw a 20 dp icon centred inside it
Size a text button's height to 48 and pad it horizontally, so the label can stay small
Keep only the outer box clickable, so the audit's touch-target check measures the 48 dp box, not the icon

snippets.note: size 48: the hit area
size 20: the visible icon
height 48 on a text button
the click sits on the 48 dp box

check.describe: Three small white icons and a blue Send pill; the audit has no layout_touch_target finding (compare DX-09). Resized (300, 540 wide) the 48 dp targets never shrink, which is the point: the row needs about 292 dp, so narrower than that Send is cut; wider, the toolbar keeps its start alignment.

pitfalls: Put onClick and semantics on the 48 dp box, not on the 20 dp icon canvas: the audit (and a finger) measures the clickable component's own bounds, so a clickable icon inside a big box is still a 20 dp target (DX-09)
Padding is inside a component's bounds, so the Send pill's horizontal padding is part of its hit area; a margin-like gap from spacedBy is not
The 48 dp box around an icon draws nothing and has no text, so it needs its own contentDescription
Paint is document state, not per canvas: after the Close icon's stroke paint, the next icon must set style fill again

examples.name: animated-value
examples.title: Animated value change
examples.summary: A brightness bar that glides to Low, Medium or High when a button is tapped: the bar's right edge is one animated expression {"value": "8 + @level * (componentWidth() - 8)", "anim": 0.6}.
examples.prompt: A brightness control: a horizontal bar with a round knob and three buttons (Low, Medium, High); tapping a button makes the bar glide smoothly to that level instead of jumping.
teaches: Animate any float by writing it as {"value": "<expr>", "anim": seconds}: the variable eases to each new result of the expression instead of jumping
Keep the animated value in a canvas `variable` command and let every shape read it (here the bar's right edge and the knob's centre)
Drive the target with plain valueFloatChange actions; the animation lives in the reader, not in the click
pitfalls: `anim` is ignored inside resources.variables (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U19): put the {value, anim} object where a float is parsed, such as a `variable` command
The anim object takes only a duration; its easing is the default (standard cubic). For other curves use animationSpec on a component (ANM-02) or shape the value yourself
Don't write an infix anim(...) call in an expression: only the object form is portable
Draw the track from componentWidth(), not the header width: a literal 320 leaves a stub on a wide host and overflows a narrow one; an animated expression may read componentWidth()

snippets.note: fill = {value: 8 + @level * (componentWidth() - 8), anim: 0.6}: the bar's right edge eases over 0.6 s, in whatever width the canvas gets
High: valueFloatChange level = 1

check.describe: Starts at Low (a quarter of the bar). A tap on High at 0.1 s, captured 0.25 s later, shows the bar mid-glide at about 70 %; it settles full width by 0.7 s. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the track spans the width and the three buttons share it by weight, so the same High tap glides to the same fraction.

examples.name: easing-gallery
examples.title: Easing gallery
examples.summary: Six dots race across their tracks when tapped, each with its own animationSpec motionEasing (Linear, Standard, Accelerate, Decelerate, Anticipate, Overshoot), so the curves can be compared mid-flight.
examples.prompt: Show the six built-in easing curves side by side: six labelled tracks, each with a dot; tapping anywhere sends every dot to the other end, each easing differently, and tapping again brings them back.
teaches: Pick a component's motion curve with animationSpec motionEasing: LINEAR, STANDARD, ACCELERATE, DECELERATE, ANTICIPATE or OVERSHOOT

Move a component by changing layout, not by drawing: a spacer with width "@go * (componentWidth() - 22)" (the track's inner width when @go is 1) pushes the dot, and the dot's animationSpec animates its new position
Toggle a 0/1 float with valueFloatExpressionChange "1 - @go" to replay the animation both ways
pitfalls: animationSpec animates the component that carries it: the spacer jumps to its new width, the dot (with the spec) glides. Put the spec on what should move
ANTICIPATE dips below the start and OVERSHOOT passes the end: leave room in the track, or clip it as here
motionDuration is in milliseconds (1200), unlike the anim object's seconds

Size the travel with an exact width: Java resolves a variable only in an exact width/height (DimensionModifierOperation.updateVariables), so fillMaxWidth "@go" is a NaN fraction there, a full fill, and the dots never move (C++ and TypeScript did resolve it). The spacer is {"width": "@go * (componentWidth() - 22)"}: in a modifier componentWidth() is the parent's full width (the track, padded 3 + 19), so every size travels the whole track. windowWidth() would not do: in Java it is the header width, not the view's

In Java a bounds animation ends at the first frame its eased progress reaches 1, without snapping to the target: OVERSHOOT stops at its overshoot (about 9% past the end here, inside the 19 dp of track padding) until the next layout; C++ settles at the end

snippets.note: animationSpec {motionDuration: 1200, motionEasing: OVERSHOOT} on the dot
the same dot with ANTICIPATE: pulls back first
spacer width @go * (componentWidth() - 22): the layout change that the dot animates, the whole inner track at any size
onClick: go = 1 - go

check.describe: A tap at 0.1 s, captured 0.4 s into the 1.2 s race: Overshoot and Decelerate lead, Standard and Linear are mid-track, Accelerate lags and Anticipate has barely left (it pulled back first). All reach the right end by 1.3 s. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) every track fills the row and each dot travels the whole track: the spacer is @go * (componentWidth() - 22), the track's inner width, with 19 dp of right padding to park the 16 dp dot.

examples.name: staggered-entrance
examples.title: Staggered list entrance
examples.summary: Five reminder rows slide in from the right and fade up one after another when the list appears: each row's graphicsLayer translationX and alpha read the same eased progress of animationTime(), delayed 0.12 s per row, and a wakeIn keeps frames coming for the 1.4 s intro.
examples.prompt: A 'This week' list of five reminders that animates in when it appears: each row slides in from the right and fades in, starting a little after the one above.
teaches: Stagger items by giving each the same progress clamp(0, 1, (animationTime() - delay_i) / 0.5) with a growing delay
Slide and fade a whole row with one graphicsLayer: translationX 48 * square(1 - p) and alpha p
Schedule frames only while the intro runs with wakeIn "0.016 + 3600 * step(animationTime(), 1.4)": every frame until 1.4 s, then an hour
pitfalls: animationTime() alone never schedules a repaint (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U6): without the wakeIn the Java player can leave the rows invisible; continuousSec() would repaint forever
step(x, edge) is x > edge, so step(animationTime(), 1.4) is 0 during the intro and 1 after
Weights ignore spacedBy (U3): the rows use a fixed spacer between the dot and the weighted title
graphicsLayer translation moves only the drawing, not the layout, so the sliding rows don't push their neighbours or overflow the column's clip

Give the weighted title maxLines 1 and ellipsis: on a narrow host it should shorten, not wrap or push the time out of the row (the C++ player still measures a weighted text at its natural width; TS and Java ellipsize)

snippets.note: row 4: translationX = 48 * (1 - p)², p = clamp(0, 1, (animationTime() - 0.66) / 0.5)
the row's graphicsLayer: alpha p and translationX from the same p
wakeIn: 60 fps for the first 1.4 s, then idle

check.describe: Captured at 0.75 s: Dentist is in place, Gym class and Team sync are still sliding and faint, Pick up parcel has just appeared to the right, Call mum is not there yet. By 1.4 s all five rows are in place. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the rows fill the width, the time stays right-aligned and a long title ellipsizes (maxLines 1) instead of pushing it; the 48 dp slide-in is a fixed distance on purpose.

examples.name: ping-pong-loop
examples.title: Ping-pong loading loop
examples.summary: A syncing card with two endless loops from continuousSec(): a puck that glides back and forth along a track (a triangle wave eased with smooth_step) and three dots that bounce in turn (phase-shifted sines).
examples.prompt: A 'Syncing photos' card with a looping progress animation: a glowing puck sliding back and forth along a track, slowing at each end, and three bouncing dots under it.
teaches: Turn a clock into a 0→1→0 ping-pong with abs((continuousSec() / 1.5) % 2 - 1) and soften the ends with smooth_step(x, 1, 0)
Stagger a loop by phase: sin(continuousSec() * 7.5 - i * 0.9) inside a loop gives each dot its own beat, and max(0, …) keeps only the hop
Use continuousSec() for endless motion: it is what schedules the repaint
pitfalls: smooth_step takes (value, max, min): smooth_step(x, 1, 0) is the usual smoothstep(0, 1, x)
continuousSec() repaints every frame for as long as the document is shown: fine for a loading state, wasteful for a static card (DX-05)
The render tool's clock has whole-second resolution: pin a clock such as 10:00:01 to get a mid-swing frame
Scale the travel with componentWidth(): a literal 280 dp swing on a 336 dp track stops short on a wide host and runs off a narrow one

snippets.note: swing = abs((continuousSec() / 1.5) % 2 - 1): a 3 s triangle wave
px = 40 + (componentWidth() - 80) * smooth_step(@swing, 1, 0): eased at both ends, across whatever width the canvas gets
three dots hopping with phase-shifted sines

check.describe: At 10:00:01 the puck is about a quarter along the track, moving left, and the first dot is up with the others lower; at 10:00:00 the puck is at the right end. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the track spans the canvas less 24 dp each side, the puck swings across all of it and the dots stay centred.

examples.name: animated-resize
examples.title: Animated card resize
examples.summary: An order card that grows to show its delivery details when tapped: its height is an expression of @open and animationSpec animates the resize, the card below slides down with its own spec, and the details fade in through an animated graphicsLayer alpha.
examples.prompt: A list of two order cards; tapping the first one expands it smoothly to show the courier, delivery window and instructions, pushing the second card down, and tapping again collapses it.
teaches: Resize a component from a variable (height "68 + @open * 78") and add animationSpec to make the new size animate instead of snapping
Give siblings their own animationSpec so they glide to their new positions as the card grows
Fade the revealed content with graphicsLayer alpha {"value": "@open", "anim": 0.4} while the box grows
pitfalls: Each component animates only if it carries animationSpec: without one on the second card it jumps down while the first card grows

A collapsed card still lays out its hidden lines below the visible area: clip the card and fade those lines (alpha 0), or they peek out under the padding. While collapsed they are squeezed to zero height, which the audit reports as layout_zero_size (expected here)
motionDuration is in milliseconds; the anim object's duration is in seconds
A card with a fixed collapsed height must keep its title on one line (maxLines 1, ellipsis): wrapped on a narrow host it pushes the subtitle out of the card

snippets.note: animationSpec {motionDuration: 450, motionEasing: DECELERATE} on the growing card
height = 68 + @open * 78
the second card's own spec: it slides down instead of jumping
details alpha {value: @open, anim: 0.4}

check.describe: A tap on the first card at 0.1 s, captured 0.1 s later: the card is most of the way to its expanded height (decelerating), the details are fading in and the Delivered card has moved down. Settled after 0.5 s. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) both cards fill the width and grow the same 78 dp; on the narrow host the title ellipsizes on one line instead of wrapping out of the 68 dp collapsed card.

examples.name: enter-exit
examples.title: Enter and exit animations
examples.summary: A notification list where tapping a notification slides it away to the right before the others close the gap (exitSequence BEFORE), and Restore opens the gaps first and then fades the notifications back in (enterSequence AFTER).
examples.prompt: Show three notifications; tapping one dismisses it by sliding it off to the right, then the ones below move up. A Restore button brings them all back with a fade.
teaches: Animate a component in and out of visibility with animationSpec enterAnimation / exitAnimation (FADE_IN, FADE_OUT, SLIDE_LEFT/RIGHT/TOP/BOTTOM, ROTATE) and visibilityDuration
Order the exit against the layout with exitSequence BEFORE (play the exit, then let siblings close the gap) and enterSequence AFTER (open the gap, then play the entrance)
Hide with an int variable read by visibility (1 visible, 0 gone) and valueIntegerChange; restoring sets all of them back to 1
pitfalls: visibility reads an integer variable: declare it with vtype int and change it with valueIntegerChange
Every list item needs its own animationSpec, including the ones that only move: the motion of the survivors comes from their specs

snippets.note: animationSpec: enter FADE_IN after the gap opens, exit SLIDE_RIGHT before the gap closes, 350 ms
visibility @n2 (int)
dismiss: n2 = 0
Restore: n1 = n2 = n3 = 1

check.describe: A tap on 'Your ride is here' at 0.1 s, captured 0.15 s later. The row is about halfway off to the right and Battery has not moved yet (BEFORE); after the 350 ms exit, Battery moves up into the gap (Java, C++ and TS alike). Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the rows fill the width, Restore stays at the right, and the dismissed row slides out by its own width.

examples.name: custom-visibility
examples.title: Custom visibility animation
examples.summary: A promo banner whose entrance and exit are drawn by two defineVisibilityAnimation functions: riseIn fades it in while it rises 60 % of its height, shrinkOut fades it while it scales down to 80 % about its centre; animationSpec names them as enterFunction and exitFunction.
examples.prompt: A 'Show offer' button that reveals a promo banner which rises and fades into place; tapping the banner dismisses it by shrinking and fading it away.
teaches: Define a transition once with defineVisibilityAnimation {name, params [progress, w, h, x, y], commands}; it runs every frame of the transition with progress 0→1
Draw the component yourself inside it: set paint alpha, translate or scale about (@x + @w / 2, @y + @h / 2), then drawComponentContent
Attach the functions with animationSpec enterFunction / exitFunction (enterAnimation and exitAnimation default to CUSTOM) and set the easing with visibilityEasing
pitfalls: defineVisibilityAnimation goes at the root, before the components that use it (a first-pass definition, like variable)
Exit progress also runs 0→1: write the exit as 1 - progress for alpha, not progress
drawComponentContent composites the component in a layer with the current paint alpha, so a paint alpha fades the whole subtree at once

snippets.note: riseIn: alpha = progress, translate dy = (1 - progress) * h * 0.6, drawComponentContent
shrinkOut: alpha 1 - progress, scale 1 - 0.2·progress about the centre
animationSpec {visibilityDuration: 500, visibilityEasing: DECELERATE, enterFunction: riseIn, exitFunction: shrinkOut}

check.describe: A tap on Show offer at 0.1 s, captured 0.2 s later. The banner is partly faded and still below its final place, rising into it; fully in place and opaque by 0.6 s. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the banner fills the width and wraps its lines on the narrow host; the rise distance is 60 % of the banner's own height (@h), so it scales with it.

examples.name: state-expand
examples.title: Mini player expands (StateLayout)
examples.summary: A now-playing mini player that expands to a full card: a stateLayout switches between a row state and a column state, and the components that carry the same animationSpec animationId in both states (the card, the album art, the title, the artist) morph from one state's bounds to the other's.
examples.prompt: A music mini player (album art, title, artist, play icon in one row); tapping it expands into a full card with big album art, the title and a progress bar, the art growing into place; tapping again collapses it.
teaches: Hold alternative layouts as children of a stateLayout and pick one with indexId (an integer variable): state 0 the row, state 1 the column

Pair the components that exist in both states with the same animationSpec animationId ({"animationSpec": {"animationId": 101, "motionDuration": 450}}) so they morph (position and size) instead of fading out and in
Put an onClick on each state's root that sets the other state (valueIntegerChange sel = 1 or 0), and an animationSpec on the stateLayout for the container's own resize
pitfalls: indexId must be an integer variable (vtype integer) changed with valueIntegerChange

The `id` modifier (component id) does not pair components across states: only animationSpec animationId does. Sharing an `id` between the two state roots even breaks the taps (the hidden state's action runs too), so leave the roots' component ids distinct
An onClick on the stateLayout itself is not dispatched by Java: put it on the state roots
Player status (2026-10-29): C++ matches Java's layout and morph; the TS player does not dispatch a tap on a state root, so it stays collapsed
Draw a progress line from componentWidth() (right = componentWidth() * 0.4), not a literal 280/112: the card is as wide as the host

snippets.note: animationSpec on the stateLayout: 450 ms STANDARD morph
indexId @sel: which child state is shown
animationId 101 on the 150 dp art; the 48 dp art in state 0 has animationId 101 too, so it grows into place
collapsed state's root: sel = 1

check.describe: A tap on the mini player at 0.1 s, captured 0.2 s later. Mid-morph: the card about two thirds of its expanded height and the art about 110 dp, moving to the centre, the title following below it. Settles to the full card with 150 dp art, title, artist and a progress bar. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540, captured settled at 1 s) the expanded card fills the width with the art centred, and the progress line is 40 % of whatever width it gets (componentWidth()); the 288 dp card needs a host at least 320 dp tall.

examples.name: play-pause-morph
examples.title: Play/pause icon morph
examples.summary: A play button whose triangle morphs into two pause bars: pathTween interpolates between two four-point paths with a tween of {"value": "@playing", "anim": 0.35}, and a tap flips @playing.
examples.prompt: A round play button that morphs smoothly into a pause icon when tapped, and back to play on the next tap.
teaches: Morph between two paths with pathTween {id, path1, path2, tween}, then draw the result by its id with drawPath
Animate the morph by making the tween an anim object: {"value": "@playing", "anim": 0.35}
Build both shapes with the same commands in the same order: the play triangle is split into two quads to match the two pause bars, corner for corner
pitfalls: The two paths must have the same verbs and point count, or the tween has nothing to pair up
An SVG string in resources.paths becomes an empty path in Java (U11): use the op list (moveTo/lineTo/close objects)
json2rc also accepts {"data": [...]} in resources.paths; Java throws a ClassCastException on it, so stay with the op list
The TS player does not draw pathTween results (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS T16)
Paths in resources.paths have fixed coordinates: centre them with one translate from componentWidth()/componentHeight() rather than drawing at the header's 180, 90

snippets.note: pathTween icon = play ↔ pause, tween {value: @playing, anim: 0.35}
play as two quads, ordered like the pause bars
playing = 1 - playing

check.describe: A tap at 0.1 s, captured 0.15 s later: halfway between play and pause, two slanted quads. Settles to two pause bars by 0.5 s. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540×260) the button and caption stay centred: one translate by (componentWidth() / 2 - 180, componentHeight() / 2 - 110) moves the whole drawing, so the paths keep their header coordinates.

examples.name: spring-switch
examples.title: Springy switches
examples.summary: Two settings switches whose thumbs spring across with a little overshoot (a graphicsLayer translationX over an animated progress, at paint time) while the blue track fades in with the same progress.
examples.prompt: A settings card with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth switches; tapping a row flips its switch with a springy thumb that slightly overshoots and a track colour that fades between grey and blue.
teaches: Animate a state change at paint time: a root variable {"value": "@on", "anim": 0.3} eases from 0 to 1 whenever @on flips, and every visual reads it
Give the thumb a spring feel with an expression over that progress: x = 22 * (p + 0.5 * sin(pi * p) * (2 * @on - 1)) overshoots about 10% and settles, in graphicsLayer translationX (no layout runs)
Cross-fade the track colour by stacking an 'on' layer whose graphicsLayer alpha is the same progress
pitfalls: JSON has no colour expression: fade between colours with an overlay's alpha

A {value, anim} animation has only the standard cubic easing; an overshoot is an expression over the eased progress, and the sine term flips sign with the target, so a tap during the 0.3 s travel jumps the thumb by up to 2 dp

Do not move the thumb with a layout dimension and an OVERSHOOT animationSpec: Java re-measures a width bound to a variable, but its bounds animation stops at the first frame the eased progress reaches 1, so an overshooting easing leaves the thumb at the overshoot (about 2 dp past the end) until the next layout (U, see EXAMPLES_FINDINGS)
Weights ignore spacedBy (U3): the text column takes weight 1 and the switch sits after it with no spacedBy

snippets.note: btP = {value: @bt, anim: 0.3}: the eased progress
thumb translationX: 22 * (p + 0.5 sin(pi p)(2 @bt - 1)), the overshoot
blue track alpha @btP

check.describe: Wi-Fi on, Bluetooth off. A tap on the Bluetooth row at 0.1 s, captured 0.08 s later: its thumb is past the middle and the track half blue. Settled after 0.6 s. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the rows fill the width with the switches pinned right; a switch keeps its 52 dp track, so its 22 dp thumb travel is a fixed distance by design.

examples.name: counting-number
examples.title: Counting number
examples.summary: A savings balance that counts up to its new total when + $250 is tapped: one animated variable {"value": "@total", "anim": 0.9} feeds both the textFromFloat label and the progress bar.
examples.prompt: A savings goal card showing the balance in large digits and a progress bar; tapping '+ $250' adds a deposit and the number counts up to the new total while the bar grows.
teaches: Count a displayed number up or down by animating a copy of it: shown = {"value": "@total", "anim": 0.9} and the label shows round(@shown)
Keep the real value exact and animate only what's displayed: the click adds to @total, the text and bar read @shown
Declare the animated copy once, at the tree root, so every reader shares the same animation
pitfalls: Round the animated value (round(@shown)) or the label shows fractional dollars while it counts
Size `whole` in textFromFloat for the largest total you expect: digits beyond it are lost
Scale the bar by componentWidth(), not the header's 320: min(1, @shown / 4000) * componentWidth() fills any width

snippets.note: shown = {value: @total, anim: 0.9}
textFromFloat(round(@shown)), 5 digits
+ $250: total = total + 250

check.describe: Starts at $1250. A tap on + $250 at 0.1 s, captured 0.3 s later, shows about $1364 and a slightly longer bar; it settles at $1500. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the bar spans the width (min(1, @shown / 4000) * componentWidth()) and the button stays at the right, so the same tap grows the bar by the same fraction.

examples.name: like-pop
examples.title: Like button pop
examples.summary: A heart that pops when tapped: the tap records animationTime() in @tapAt and toggles @liked; the heart's scale overshoots and settles from the time since the tap, an impulse starting at @tapAt draws an expanding ring, and a wakeIn asks for frames only during the 0.6 s pop.
examples.prompt: A like button: tapping the outlined heart fills it red with a quick pop (it grows and settles back) and a ring that bursts outward; tapping again un-likes it.
teaches: Start a one-shot animation from a tap by storing the tap time: valueFloatExpressionChange tapAt = animationTime(), then p = clamp(0, 1, (animationTime() - @tapAt) / 0.45)
Pop with scale 1.6 + 0.5 · sin(π·p) · (1 - p): up fast, back to rest exactly when p reaches 1
Draw extra effects only during the pop with an impulse whose start is @tapAt, and request frames with wakeIn only until it ends
pitfalls: animationTime() alone never repaints (U6) and an impulse asks for no repaint: the wakeIn "0.016 + 3600 * step(animationTime() - @tapAt, 0.6)" supplies the frames
Initialise tapAt in the past (-10) so nothing pops on load
An impulseProcess skips the first frame of its window; keep the main shape (the heart) outside the impulse so it is always drawn
Centre a drawing made at the header's coordinates with one translate from componentWidth()/componentHeight(): the host may give the canvas any size

snippets.note: onClick: liked = 1 - liked, tapAt = animationTime()
s = 1.6 + 0.5 sin(πp)(1 - p): the pop
impulse 0.5 s from @tapAt: the expanding ring
wakeIn every frame for 0.6 s after the tap

check.describe: A tap on the heart at 0.2 s, captured 0.15 s later: the heart is filled red and larger than at rest, with a ring around it. After 0.6 s it rests filled at normal size, with no ring. Pick a variant with a static param (style: filled / outlined / text, enabled: false)
Fill a component slot (icon) with your own content
Re-colour one instance with a theme colour (color: "@colors.error")

snippets.note: the minimal call: label plus an onClick action
a slot: the icon content goes in slots.icon
enabled: false dims it, drops the click, and marks the semantics disabled

pitfalls: Disabled is a static variant (enabled: false): the click and ripple are left out at build time and the semantics say disabled, so it cannot be toggled at run time; for a button that becomes enabled, stack two buttons and switch with visibility

the On/Off status: two texts faded by the 0/1 state
a Checkbox: its label is both the visible text and the accessibility label
unbound: the checkbox keeps its own state

The status canvas and the switch are separated by fixed spacer boxes, not spacedBy: the row holds a weight, and weights ignore spacedBy
An unbound component gets a fresh per-call variable (checkbox1_checked): nothing else in the document can read it, so bind a variable as soon as anything depends on the state

-50 to 50: min and max can be negative
reads @volume after the slider: the dragged value
the slider's label is its accessibility label; the visible name is the text above it

examples.name: chips-badges
examples.title: Chips and badges
examples.summary: Six library Chips wrapping in a flow (Travel and Music preset through document variables, the rest keeping their own state) and Badges: a count, a live unread count from a host variable, 999+, New and Beta.

teaches: Toggle a filter with {"Chip": {"label": ..., "selected": "@travel"}}; leave selected out and it keeps its own
Wrap chips onto lines with flow; the gaps come from end/bottom padding on a wrapper box, since flow ignores spacedBy
Show a live count with {"Badge": {"count": "@unread"}}, or fixed text with {"Badge": {"text": "New"}}

snippets.note: a Chip bound to @travel (selected)
chips in a flow with padded wrappers
a Badge bound to @unread

pitfalls: flow ignores spacedBy (Java and the players alike): wrap each chip in a box with end and bottom padding, which also keeps the first chip aligned with the text above
A chip with no `selected` variable still toggles, but nothing else can read its state: bind a variable for every filter the document (or host) acts on
Badge count uses textFromFloat with whole 4 and flags 5: fewer whole digits drop the leading ones (whole 1 prints 12 as 2); a count above 9999 should be text such as 999+
A flow grows taller as the host narrows: content that fits at the header width can then run past the bottom, so make the page scroll (verticalScroll on the root column)

check.describe: Travel and Music start selected; tapping Photography selects it; variables {unread: 3} shows 3 in the second badge. Resized, the chips re-flow to the width: one line at 540 wide, three at 234, where the badges move below the fold and the page scrolls (verticalScroll) instead of overflowing.

examples.prompt: Build a contacts screen with an app bar and a search button, and a scrolling card listing people with coloured initials avatars, names, subtitles and a chevron, where tapping a row opens it.
teaches: Compose a screen from components: TopBar, Card, ListItem, Avatar, Divider
Fill slots with other components (an Avatar in leading) or your own drawing (the search icon button in the TopBar actions)
Line rows up inside a Card: ListItem padding 0 (the card already pads) and Divider inset 56 (40 dp avatar + 16)
Make the area under a top bar scroll: verticalWeight 1 plus verticalScroll bound to a variable

snippets.note: a ListItem with an Avatar in its leading slot, the built-in chevron and a click
the scrolling area under the top bar: verticalWeight 1 + verticalScroll
a TopBar with an icon button labelled Search in its actions slot
an inset Divider between rows

check.describe: Tapping the second row sets opened to 2; tapping Search sets it to 99; dragging up scrolls the card under the top bar to the fifth row. Resized, the top bar and the card fill the width with the chevrons at the end; at 234 wide a long name (Katherine Johnson) wraps onto two lines and the list still scrolls.

A ListItem pads itself by 16 dp; inside a Card, which pads too, pass padding: 0 or the avatars sit 32 dp in from the card title
Divider inset is measured from the row start: padding + 56 lines it up with the title after a 40 dp Avatar
An icon-only button needs its own semantics contentDescription (Search): the canvas inside it has no text for accessibility

examples.name: tabs-pager
examples.title: Tabs and page dots
examples.summary: The library Tabs bound to a document variable that three stacked panels (Cards) and PagerDots follow: tapping a tab shows its panel and moves the dot.
examples.prompt: Make a Day / Week / Month tab bar that switches a summary card below it, with page dots that follow the selected tab.
teaches: Switch views with {"Tabs": {"labels": [...], "selected": "@tab"}}: the labels are static, the selection a variable
Show one of several stacked panels by fading each with graphicsLayer alpha 1 - min(1, abs(@tab - i))
Follow the same variable with {"PagerDots": {"count": 3, "current": "@tab"}}

snippets.note: Tabs bound to @tab
the Week panel, visible when @tab is 1

pitfalls: Panels faded with graphicsLayer alpha still take their space and receive taps; for a panel with controls, use visibility instead
The stacked panels sit in one box, so the box is as tall as the tallest panel: keep them the same height or the shorter ones float above empty space
1 - min(1, abs(@tab - i)) is 1 only for the selected index; with an animated tab variable it cross-fades neighbours, but a jump from 0 to 2 also flashes panel 1 on the way

check.describe: Starts on Day; tapping Month sets tab to 2, shows the This month card and lights the third dot. Resized, the three tabs share the width with the underline under the selected one, and the card, its bar and the dots follow: at 234 and at 540 wide.

examples.name: progress-gallery
examples.title: Progress gallery
examples.summary: The library ProgressBar and ProgressRing at 0, 33, 66 and 100 %, in theme colours, and a pair bound to an exported host variable.
examples.prompt: Show linear progress bars and circular progress rings at a few percentages, and one pair driven by a download progress value the host app sets.
teaches: Show progress with {"ProgressBar": {"progress": 0.66}}: the fill follows the bar's own measured width
Draw a ring with {"ProgressRing": {"progress": ...}}; size, thickness and showLabel are static variants
Drive both from one exported host variable ("progress": "@download")

snippets.note: a ProgressBar at 33 % inside a weighted box
a ProgressRing with a theme colour
ring and bar bound to @download

check.describe: Bars fill 0/33/66/100 % of their track and the rings read 0, 33, 66 and 100; with variables {download: 0.9} the bottom pair is nearly full. Resized, the bars stretch with the width and the four 48 dp rings are spread with spaceEvenly, so they all still fit at 234 wide and spread out at 540; the caption ellipsizes on one line.

pitfalls: A ProgressBar fills its parent width: in a row give it a weighted box (weight 1), or it has no width to measure
The bar fill is max(height, width × progress), so 0 % still shows a round dot; hide the bar (visibility) if 0 must show nothing
ProgressRing does not clamp: a literal progress folds to a constant sweep at build time, but a host value above 1 draws a full ring and a label over 100
Only exported variables ({"value": 0.42, "export": true}) can be set by the host; a plain number is private to the document
ProgressRing has a fixed size: a row of four 64 dp rings with a 14 dp spacedBy overflows a narrower host. Spread smaller rings with horizontalArrangement spaceEvenly, sized for the narrowest host

examples.name: gauges-stats
examples.title: Gauges and KPI tiles
examples.summary: The library Gauge in its green, amber and red zones (CPU bound to a host variable) and two StatTile KPIs: revenue from host variables with a rising delta, and churn with invert: true so its fall shows green.
examples.prompt: Make a small system dashboard with CPU, memory and disk dial gauges that turn amber and red as they fill, and KPI tiles showing revenue and churn with up/down change indicators.
teaches: Show a value on a zoned dial with {"Gauge": {"value": "@cpu", "label": "CPU %"}}
Pick a colour by a value's range or sign: overlapping draws whose paint alpha is a 0/1 step()
Say which direction is good: StatTile invert: true for metrics where lower is better (churn, latency)
Lay tiles out in equal columns: weighted boxes with a fixed spacer box between them

snippets.note: a Gauge bound to the host variable cpu
a StatTile whose delta colour is picked by its sign (invert: a fall is good)
two equal tiles: weighted boxes and a fixed spacer

check.describe: CPU green at 42, memory amber at 72, disk red at 93; with variables {cpu: 90} the first gauge turns red; revenueDelta -2 turns the revenue delta red with a down chevron; churn -0.4 is green. Resized, each gauge sits in a weighted 104 dp high box with fill: true, so the dials shrink to share the row at 252 wide and stay 104 dp (centred in their thirds) at 540; the two StatTiles share the width at any size.

pitfalls: step(x, edge) is x > edge: a delta of exactly 0 counts as a fall, and a gauge exactly at warnAt is still green
Weights ignore spacedBy: the two tiles are weighted boxes with a 12 dp spacer box between them, not a spacedBy row
A literal value (72) still compiles its zone and sweep expressions; only the host-bound gauge needs them, but the component cannot tell the two apart
Numbers are textFromFloat with flags 5; the default flags pad them with spaces and push them off centre

Three fixed 104 dp gauges need 328 dp: in a plain row a narrower host squeezes the last one to 0 wide. Pass fill: true and give each call a weighted box with a height; put the gaps in padding, since weights ignore spacedBy

examples.name: charts-gallery
examples.title: Charts from one dataset
examples.summary: The library Sparkline, BarChart and DonutChart all reading the same exported 8-value float array: a trend line beside its label, labelled weekly columns that fill the card, and a ring of the weeks' shares with the total in the centre. Setting the array redraws all three.
examples.prompt: Show eight weeks of visits three ways from one dataset: a sparkline next to its label, a bar chart with week labels, and a donut with the total in the middle. The host should be able to push new numbers.
teaches: Declare the data once as an exported float array (resources.floatArrays) and pass its name to every chart: {"BarChart": {"values": "@visits"}}
A host that sets the array (render_rc variables {visits: [...]}) redraws every chart, at any length, with no new document

Charts scale to their box: Sparkline beside a weighted label at 120 × 32, BarChart with fill: true in a box with verticalWeight 1 (the height that is left), DonutChart with fill: true in a fixed-height box

In a column, give the stretching child verticalWeight: plain weight is horizontal, and in a column it leaves the box 0 wide (with fillMaxWidth before it) or lets it take the whole height, pushing the next children out. Weights ignore spacedBy, so the gaps are top paddings

snippets.note: the one dataset, exported so the host can replace it
Sparkline reading @visits
BarChart: one bar per value, in a loop over the array
DonutChart: one arc per value, the canvas rotated after each
verticalWeight: the bar chart takes the height that is left

visits.meaning: weekly visits, oldest first; values >= 0, any length (the bar labels stay W1..W8)

check.describe: A rising blue sparkline ending on a dot at 84; eight blue columns W1..W8 rising to W8; a ring of eight slices from solid to pale blue with 490 visits in the centre. With variables {visits: [90, 75, 80, 50, 40, 45, 30, 20]} all three change: the line and the bars fall, the first slices grow and the total reads 430. At 252 and 540 dp wide the line and bars follow the width and the ring stays centred at 120 dp.

pitfalls: values is a float array's name, not a JSON list: an inline [42, 55, ...] cannot be replaced by the host and the charts' loops need arrayGet
The bar labels are written when the document is built: a host can send new numbers but not new labels, so keep the array 8 long, or drop labels
Each chart rescales to its own data (the sparkline to min..max, the bars to 0..max, the ring to the sum): they agree on shape, not on a shared axis

examples.name: time-gallery
examples.title: Clock gallery
examples.summary: The library AnalogClock (with and without a second hand) and DigitalClock (24-hour with seconds, 12-hour), all from the host clock.
examples.prompt: Show the current time as two analog clock faces, one with a second hand, and as a digital clock in 24-hour format with seconds and in 12-hour format.
teaches: Drop in a clock face with {"AnalogClock": {"size": 150}}; showSeconds false repaints once a minute
Show the time with {"DigitalClock": {"format": "12h", "showSeconds": true}}
Static params (size, format) shape the expanded drawing; colours stay theme references

snippets.note: an AnalogClock with a second hand
a 12-hour DigitalClock

check.describe: At 22:10:05 the hands show 10:10 (the first clock with its second hand at 5 s), the 24 h clock reads 22:10:05 and the 12 h one 10:10. Resized, each clock sits in a weighted 150 dp high box with fill: true: at 234 wide both faces shrink to about 89 dp side by side, at 540 they stay 150 dp centred in their halves; the digital clocks stay centred.

pitfalls: timeInMin() is minutes since midnight but timeInSec() is the second within the hour (605 at 10:10:05): the hour hand uses timeInMin() % 720, the minute and second fields % 60
A clock showing seconds repaints every second; without them, once a minute. Leave seconds off on an ambient or battery-sensitive surface
The 12-hour hour is (floor(timeInHr()) + 11) % 12 + 1 (1..12, no zero pad) and there is no AM/PM marker: add one if the time of day is ambiguous
Render checks need a pinned clock (check.render.clock); otherwise every run reads the wall clock

Two fixed 150 dp clocks need 324 dp: in a plain row a narrower host cuts the second one off. Pass fill: true and give each call a weighted box with a height; put the gap in padding (12 dp each side), since weights ignore spacedBy

examples.name: status-gallery
examples.title: Status gallery
examples.summary: The library WeatherIcon in every condition, BatteryIndicator at the host battery level and at 95, 40 and 10 % (green, amber, red), and Banner in its info, warn and error kinds.
examples.prompt: Show status symbols: a weather icon for sunny, cloudy, rain, snow and storm, labelled; battery indicators for the device's battery and for 95, 40 and 10 percent, coloured by level; and an info, a warning and an error banner.
teaches: {"WeatherIcon": {"condition": "storm", "size": 40}}: five static conditions, drawn with circles, rounded rects and lines
{"BatteryIndicator": {"level": "@battery"}} follows an exported host float; literal levels fold to numbers, so the 95/40/10 icons cost no variable
The battery colour is green, amber below 50 and red with a ! below 20, chosen by conditionalOperations: the low render (battery = 10) turns the host icon red
{"Banner": {"text": ..., "kind": "warn"}} frames a message in the kind's colour with its own icon shape; each unbound banner keeps its own visible variable, and dismissible: false drops the cross

snippets.note: the five weather conditions in weighted columns
the battery bound to the host level
10 %: red, with a !
a warn Banner

check.describe: Five distinct weather icons (an amber sun with rays, a grey cloud, a cloud with blue drops, a cloud with blue dots, a cloud with an amber bolt), each labelled. Battery icons: the host level 76 (green, three quarters), 95 (green), 40 (amber), 10 (red with a !). Three banners: info (blue, circled i, with a cross), warn (amber, triangle, with a cross) and error (red, circled !, no cross). With battery = 10 (the low render) the first battery turns red, shows the ! and reads 10%. WeatherIcon's condition is static: a host-chosen condition needs the five icons behind a stateLayout or visibility

examples.title: Settings rows

Clamp a counter with Stepper (min, max, step), bound to a variable other parts read (the Details card's Guests line)
Nest components: a Stepper and a Switch in KeyValueRow trailing slots, inside a Card's content

snippets.note: a Stepper (1..4) in a KeyValueRow trailing slot
a KeyValueRow whose value is a live textFromFloat
a Switch in a KeyValueRow trailing slot

a Card holding a Switch row and a Checkbox

a Switch in the row's trailing slot, starting on, with its own state

the document-level description a screen reader announces

examples.name: desired-fps
examples.title: Desired frame rate
examples.summary: A dot that slides across a track every 2 s, in a document whose header asks the player for 30 fps.

Map the 0..1 phase onto a track: x = 30 + phase * 240
Paint the canvas background with a background modifier instead of a full-size drawRect

cx = 30 + (continuousSec() % 2) / 2 * 240: one pass every 2 s

examples.prompt: Content drawn entirely outside the canvas.

Fix it by drawing in canvas coordinates (0..componentWidth(), 0..componentHeight())

snippets.note: the flaw: a circle centred at (450, 320), past both edges

examples.name: operators
examples.title: Operators and precedence
examples.summary: Seven formulas over two exported variables (a = 7, b = 3) with their live results: precedence, parentheses, left-to-right evaluation, float division, % and unary minus.
examples.prompt: Show a small cheat sheet of arithmetic formulas over a = 7 and b = 3 (a + b * 2, (a + b) * 2, a - b - 1, a / b, a % b, -a % b, -b * -2) with each computed result next to it.
teaches: Write a value as an infix formula string over @variables: "@a + @b * 2" compiles to one float expression that re-evaluates when a or b changes
Rely on the usual precedence (* / % before + -, unary minus binds tightest) and group with parentheses; equal operators run left to right
Expect % to truncate like Java's float %: the result takes the sign of the left operand, so -7 % 3 is -1, not 2
pitfalls: The infix parser knows only + - * / % and unary minus: no ^, no comparison (<, >, ==) and no && or ||; write pow(x, n), and step() or ifElse() for comparisons (EXP-06)
Write a variable as @name; a bare name also resolves when it is declared, but bare width and height mean componentWidth() and componentHeight(), so don't name your own variables that and drop the @
-3 directly after an operator, a comma or a parenthesis is folded into a negative literal; -@b is a CHANGE_SIGN operation on the variable
A device reader refuses an expression longer than 32 RPN tokens (numbers, variables, operators and functions each count); split a long formula into named resources.variables

When a row of formula, result and note no longer fits, a plain row squeezes the last child to 0 wide: make it a collapsibleRow and give the note a collapsiblePriority (1) so it is the one dropped; unprioritized children are kept first

snippets.note: a exported (export: true) so the host can change it; every formula below follows
@a + @b * 2 → 13: * binds before +
-@a % @b → -1: % keeps the sign of the left side
textFromFloat with decimal 2 and flags 7 shows 2.33

check.describe: Seven rows read 13, 20, 3, 2.33, 1, -1 and 6. Resized, the rows fill the width; each row is a collapsibleRow whose note has the lowest priority, so at 234 wide the notes are dropped while every formula keeps its result, and at 540 the notes have room to spare.

examples.name: math-library
examples.title: Math function reference
examples.summary: Sixteen expression functions evaluated on sample arguments (sqrt, pow, exp, ln, log, hypot, square, atan2, floor, ceil, round, fract, abs, sign, max), each shown with its result.
examples.prompt: Make a reference card of RemoteCompose's math functions: show sqrt(2), pow(2, 10), exp(1), ln(10), log(1000), hypot(3, 4), square(1.5), atan2(1, 1), floor/ceil/round/fract of negative numbers, abs, sign and max, each with its value.
teaches: Call the math functions inside any expression string: sqrt, pow(x, n), exp, ln (natural), log (base 10), hypot(x, y), square, floor, ceil, round, fract, abs, sign, min, max
Check rounding on negative numbers: floor(-2.5) is -3, ceil(-2.5) is -2, fract(-2.25) is -0.25 (x minus its truncation)
Print a computed value with textFromFloat; flags 519 (7 + 512 OPTIONS_ROUNDING) rounds the last decimal instead of cutting it
pitfalls: log is base 10 and ln is natural: log(1000) = 3, ln(10) = 2.303
round is Java's Math.round, half rounds UP: round(-2.5) = -2 (the C++ player gives -3, see the family's findings)
mad(a, b, c) is a * b + c in the reference (and the TS player); the C++ player computes a + b * c, so mad(2, 3, 4) shows 14 instead of 10. Write a * b + c until it is fixed
The JSON parser has no deg(), rad(), cbrt(), log2(), mod() or mix(): they are runtime operators without a JSON name, and an unknown name fails with "Unknown token". Multiply by 57.29578 for degrees
atan2(y, x) returns radians: atan2(1, 1) = 0.785

Two fixed 160 dp columns need about 330 dp: in a narrower host the second column is squeezed off. Put the cells in a flow (widthIn max two cells so the columns survive a wider host) and let the page scroll

snippets.note: textFromFloat of sqrt(2), 3 decimals, rounded
ln(10): natural log
fract(-2.25) → -0.25: fract truncates
the sixteen cells in a flow capped at 328 dp (two 164 dp cells a line), so a narrower host gets one column and the page scrolls

check.describe: Sixteen cells: 1.414, 1024, 2.718, 2.303, 3, 5, 2.25, 0.785 on the left; -3, -2, 3, -2, -0.25, 4, -1, 8 on the right. Resized, the cells sit in a flow capped at two 164 dp cells a line: at 234 wide they stack in one column (powers and rounding alternating) and the page scrolls; at 540 the two columns stay together, centred.

examples.name: easing-curves
examples.title: Easing curves compared
examples.summary: Linear, ease-in (square), ease-out, smooth_step and smootherstep drawn over each other on one unit-square chart, each a pathExpression in t = a[0], with a legend.
examples.prompt: Plot five easing curves from 0 to 1 on the same chart (linear, ease in, ease out, smoothstep, smootherstep) with a colour legend and the formula under each name.
teaches: Shape a 0..1 parameter with plain expressions: square(t) eases in, 1 - square(1 - t) eases out, smooth_step(t, 1, 0) and t*t*t*(t*(6*t - 15) + 10) ease both ends
Plot y = f(t) as a pathExpression with start 0, end 1 and a[0] as t, mapping it into the box with x = left + w * t and y = bottom - h * f(t)
Reuse one id per curve ("easeIn", "smooth"…) and draw it with drawPath after setting the stroke
pitfalls: smooth_step takes (value, max, min): smooth_step(t, 1, 0) is the usual smoothstep(0, 1, t). Not clamp's order
pathExpression without flags 4 (LINEAR) joins the samples with splines; 64 linear samples are enough for these curves, a straight line needs only count 2
The JSON parser has no smoothstep, mix or ease names: write the polynomial, and keep it under 32 RPN tokens

A canvas drawn at its header size (literal coordinates) runs off a narrower host and leaves a strip in a wider one: when the drawing is one composition (chart and legend, dial and readout), scale it as a whole with @fit = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H) and centre it with a translate

snippets.note: ease in: square(a[0])
ease out: 1 - square(1 - a[0])
smooth_step(a[0], 1, 0): value first, then max, then min
smootherstep t³(t(6t − 15) + 10) as a 64-sample linear pathExpression

check.describe: Five curves from bottom-left to top-right: a grey diagonal, blue below it, green above it, yellow and red S-curves crossing at the centre, the red steeper. Resized, the chart and its legend are scaled as one (@fit = min(w / 360, h / 240)) and centred: smaller at 234 wide with the legend still beside the chart, centred at 1:1 in a 540 wide box.

examples.name: remap-ranges
examples.title: Mapping values between ranges
examples.summary: Three readings in their own units (temperature −10…40 °C, gain −60…0 dB, speed 0…120 km/h) normalised with clamp((v − lo) / (hi − lo)) and placed on tracks with lerp; the out-of-range speed pins to the end.
examples.prompt: Show temperature, audio gain and speed on horizontal tracks, each mapped from its own range onto the track, with values past the end clamped.
teaches: Normalise a value to 0..1 once, as a named expression: tTemp = clamp(0, 1, (@temp + 10) / 50)
Map the normalised t onto pixels with lerp(start, end, t): cx = lerp(20, 340, @tTemp)
Clamp before mapping so an out-of-range input (speed 140 on a 0..120 scale) pins to the end instead of drawing off the track
pitfalls: clamp takes (min, max, value): the value is LAST, clamp(x, 0, 1) is always 0 (it is min(max(a, c), b), so only the max has to be in the middle)
lerp(a, b, t) does not clamp: lerp(30, 340, 1.17) is 392, past the track, which is why t is clamped first
A gradient set on the paint stays set when you change the colour: the marker after the gradient track would be painted with the gradient. Clear it with {"shader": 0} in the next paint's ops

Tracks drawn to x = 340 only fit the 360 header width: read componentWidth() into a variable (@r) and use it for the right ends, the gradient and the lerp targets; text that only fits when wide can go in a conditionalOperations on that width

snippets.note: clamp(0, 1, @speed / 120): 140 km/h pins to 1
lerp(20, @r, @tTemp): 0..1 onto the track, whose right end @r = componentWidth() - 20 follows the live width
{"shader": 0} clears the gradient before the solid marker

check.describe: The temperature marker sits two thirds along the gradient track (23 °C), the gain bar fills 70 % (−18 dB), the speed bar is full with its thumb at the end and a red "over range" note. Resized, the tracks run from 20 px to the live width minus 20 (@r = componentWidth() - 20) and the values, the formula and the markers stay right-aligned at the same fractions, at 234 and at 540 wide; below 320 wide the formula and the over-range note are left out (a conditionalOperations on @r) so they do not run into the title and the Speed label.

examples.name: polar-trig
examples.title: Compass bearing with atan2
examples.summary: A compass dial of 60 ticks placed with sin/cos in a loop, a needle that points at an exported target with atan2, and the bearing (degrees) and distance (hypot) printed beside it.
examples.prompt: Draw a compass dial with tick marks and N/E/S/W, and a needle pointing from the centre at a target point; show the bearing in degrees and the distance to the target.
teaches: Place items around a circle from a loop index: x = cx + r * sin(i * 0.10472), y = cy − r * cos(i * 0.10472) (6° steps, 0° at the top, clockwise)
Point at a target with atan2(dx, −dy) for a compass bearing (0 at north, clockwise); keep the angle in one named variable and reuse it for both needle ends
Convert radians to 0..360 degrees with (angle * 57.29578 + 360) % 360, and measure the distance with hypot(dx, dy)
Vary a tick's length without a branch: 74 + 6 * step(i % 5, 0) is 74 every fifth tick and 80 otherwise
pitfalls: Every trig function works in radians and there is no deg() or rad() in JSON: multiply by 57.29578 or 0.0174533
atan2 takes (y, x). In screen coordinates y grows downward, so a compass bearing is atan2(dx, -dy), not atan2(dy, dx)
% of a negative angle stays negative (-90 % 360 = -90): add 360 before taking % 360

A canvas drawn at its header size (literal coordinates) runs off a narrower host and leaves a strip in a wider one: when the drawing is one composition (chart and legend, dial and readout), scale it as a whole with @fit = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H) and centre it with a translate

snippets.note: b = atan2(@tx - 110, 115 - @ty): bearing in radians
60 ticks around the dial; the long ones every fifth via step(i % 5, 0)
needle tip: 110 + 62 * sin(@b), 115 - 62 * cos(@b)
hypot(@tx - 110, @ty - 115): distance
textMerge(number, "°") keeps the unit against the digits

check.describe: The red needle points up and to the right at the yellow target; the readout says 53° and 75 px. Resized, the compass and its readout are scaled as one (@fit = min(w / 360, h / 230)) and centred: smaller at 234 wide, 1.5× at 540×345, the bearing and distance unchanged.

examples.name: branchless-select
examples.title: Branchless selection with step and ifElse
examples.summary: Three batteries (18, 42, 86 %) in a loop: red, amber or green fill chosen by step() masks used as paint alpha, a status word picked the same way, and a time estimate chosen by ifElse(left, to-full, charging).
examples.prompt: Show three battery levels from an array; colour each red below 20 %, amber up to 50 % and green above, label it Low/Medium/Good, and show minutes left, or minutes to full when that battery is charging.
teaches: Turn a comparison into a 0/1 mask with step(x, edge), which is x > edge: low = 1 − step(v, 20), mid = step(v, 20) * (1 − step(v, 50)), high = step(v, 50)
Pick a colour by drawing each candidate with its mask as paint alpha: only the one whose mask is 1 shows, with no conditional block
Choose between two numbers with ifElse(otherwise, then, condition): ifElse(v * 6, (100 − v) * 1.2, charging) is the time to full while charging, else the time left
Use max() as a lower bound instead of a branch: the fill is never thinner than 8 px
pitfalls: ifElse takes (else, then, condition), condition LAST: it returns the second argument when the third is > 0, else the first
step(x, edge) is 1 when x > edge, strictly: step(20, 20) = 0, so 20 % counts as Low here
Paint alpha set from a mask stays on the paint: reset {"alpha": 1} before the next solid drawing
Text can't change inside a loop (each label is one text id), so the per-row numbers are drawn outside the loop with arrayGet(@levels, 0…2)

Labels drawn at x = 246 fall off a host narrower than about 330 dp: when the canvas is one composition, scale it as a whole with @fit = min(componentWidth() / 360, componentHeight() / 200) and centre it with a translate

snippets.note: low mask: 1 - step(level, 20)
band mask: step(level, 20) * (1 - step(level, 50))
max(37, 29 + 1.16 * level): a minimum width without a branch
ifElse(level * 6, (100 - level) * 1.2, charging)
one loop draws the three batteries from the levels array

check.describe: Top battery 18 % red, Low, 108 min left; middle 42 % amber, Medium, 69 min to full (charging); bottom 86 % green, Good, 516 min left. Resized, the batteries, percentages and labels are scaled as one (@fit = min(w / 360, h / 200)) and centred: at 234 wide the Low / Medium / Good labels and time estimates stay visible beside smaller batteries; at 540 they are centred at 1:1.

examples.name: conditional-blocks
examples.title: Threshold categories with conditionalOperations
examples.summary: An air-quality reading whose badge and advice come from conditionalOperations blocks: eq for no data, nested gt/le pairs for each band (AND), and the scale marker from a clamped expression.
examples.prompt: Show an air quality index with a coloured category badge (Good, Moderate, Unhealthy for some, Unhealthy) and one line of advice for the band the value falls in, plus a scale with a marker.
teaches: Draw a block only when a comparison holds with conditionalOperations {condition: gt|ge|lt|le|eq, v1, v2, commands}: v1 is compared to v2
Test a band (50 < v ≤ 100) by nesting two blocks: a gt block containing a le block
Write the else branch as its own block with the complementary condition; there is no else
Keep continuous things (the marker position) as expressions and use blocks only for content that differs per band
pitfalls: There is no else, and no and/or: nest for AND, repeat the block for OR, and write the complement for else
The condition names are gt, ge, lt, le and eq (case-insensitive); anything else becomes 0, which the reader does not treat as an error
eq compares floats exactly: use it on whole numbers or flags, not on computed fractions
Static text in the blocks is fine; a value that only changes size or position is cheaper as an expression than as four blocks

A canvas laid out with literal x coordinates (98, 179, 340) only fits its header width: compute the edges from componentWidth(), and when there is less room than the design needs, scale the drawing down as a whole (min(1, componentWidth() / 360)) rather than letting text run off the edge

snippets.note: eq: only when @aqi == 0, the "No reading" note
gt 50 containing le 100: the Moderate band
gt 150 alone: the open-ended top band
20 + 4 * @q * clamp(0, 1, @aqi / 200), @q being a quarter of the live scale width
@s = min(1, componentWidth() / 360): below the 360 design width the whole card is scaled down (and centred vertically); above it @r = componentWidth() / @s - 20 stretches the scale

check.describe: AQI 132: an orange "Unhealthy for some" badge, the sensitive-groups advice, and the marker between 100 and 150 on the scale. aqi 0, 30, 75 and 180 show No reading, Good, Moderate and Unhealthy. Resized, at 234 wide the card is scaled down as a whole (@s = 0.65) and centred vertically; at 540 the scale stretches to the live width (quarters of @r - 20) while the badge stops growing at 200 px.

examples.name: array-stats
examples.title: Array statistics
examples.summary: A week of step counts from a float array: bars scaled by arrayMax, the best day highlighted by a step mask, an average line, and total, average, best and standard deviation computed with arraySum, arrayLength, arrayMax and arraySumSqr.
examples.prompt: Show a week of step counts as a bar chart with the best day highlighted and an average line, and summary stats on top: total, average, best day and standard deviation.
teaches: Aggregate an array inside expressions: arraySum(@a), arrayLength(@a), arrayMax(@a), arrayMin(@a), arrayGet(@a, i)
Compute an average once as a named variable (avg = arraySum / arrayLength) and a standard deviation as sqrt(arraySumSqr(@a) / arrayLength(@a) − square(@avg))
Highlight the maximum without a branch: alpha 0.45 + 0.55 * step(arrayGet(@a, i), arrayMax(@a) − 1)
Print large numbers with thousands separators (flags 21: 16 GROUPING_BY3 + 5) and round in the expression with round()
pitfalls: There is no arrayAvg in JSON (the runtime has one): divide arraySum by arrayLength
arrayGet takes (array, index), array first
textFromFloat with decimal 0 cuts the fraction (8385.7 prints 8385) unless the rounding flag 512 is set; round() in the expression does the same and keeps the flags simple
floatArrays are exported by default: a host can replace the week's values and every statistic follows

Bars placed at 29 + i * 45.714 only span the header width: derive the slot from componentWidth() ((@r - 20) / 7) so they spread over any width, and scale the chart down as a whole where the four figures would no longer fit

snippets.note: avg = arraySum(@steps) / arrayLength(@steps)
std dev: round(sqrt(arraySumSqr / n − square(avg)))
bars scaled by arrayGet / arrayMax; the best day's mask from step()
arraySum with flags 21 → 58,700

check.describe: Seven bars, Saturday tallest and brighter; a yellow average line at about 70 % of the tallest; the stats read 58,700 total, 8,386 average, 12,100 best day and 2,139 standard deviation. Resized, below the 360 design width the chart is scaled down as a whole (@s = min(1, w / 360)) and centred vertically, so the four figures still fit on one line at 234 wide; wider, the figures spread over quarters and the bars over sevenths of the live width (@r = componentWidth() / @s - 20), at 540 wide too.

examples.name: seeded-skyline
examples.title: Seeded random skyline
examples.summary: A night city generated from seeded randomness: 14 towers whose heights, window counts and lit windows all come from seed(n, rand()) keyed on the loop indices, under 50 seeded stars; identical on every render.
examples.prompt: Generate a night skyline: a row of towers of random heights with randomly lit windows, a moon and stars, the same picture every time.
teaches: Get a repeatable random number per item with seed(key, rand()): it reseeds the generator with key, then evaluates rand()
Recompute the same seeded value wherever it is needed (tower top, window rows, window y) instead of storing it: the same key always gives the same number
Combine nested loop indices into one key (i * 389 + j * 41 + k * 7 + 20000) for a value per window, and threshold it with step(…, 0.55) for on/off
Use seeded values in a loop's until: floor((40 + 110 * seed(…)) / 10) − 1 window rows per tower
pitfalls: Consecutive small seeds (i + 1) give first values that rise or fall in a ramp, because the seed is the float's bits: spread the keys with a multiplier (i * 97 + 3) and give x, y and size different multipliers or the stars fall on a line
rand() without seed() is different on every evaluation and every load; the C++ renderer needs --seed to pin it
A variable holding seed(…) is not a stored number but an expression; inside a loop write the seed inline with the loop index

A seeded scene drawn for a 360×200 box leaves a blank strip in a wider host: drive the loop count from componentWidth() and stand the towers on componentHeight(); since each tower is keyed by its index, the ones that were there keep their look

snippets.note: tower top: @h - 40 - 110 * seed(i * 97 + 3, rand()), standing on the live bottom edge
window rows from the same seeded height
lit or dark: 0.9 * step(seed(window key, rand()), 0.55)
50 stars with separate keys for x, y, size and brightness

check.describe: Fourteen dark towers of mixed heights with scattered amber windows, a pale moon top right and faint stars; the picture is the same on every render. Resized, the sky fills the box and the towers stand on its bottom edge: 9 towers at 234 wide, 21 at 540 (the loop runs to ceil(componentWidth() / 26)); the first towers keep their seeded heights and windows at any size, and the moon stays 60 px from the right.

examples.name: modifier-expressions
examples.title: Expressions in layout modifiers
examples.summary: A download card where layout modifiers take expressions: the bar is fillMaxWidth(@p), the percent bubble is offset by clamp(0, 280, @p * 328 − 24), equalizer bars get height from an array, and the caption fades with graphicsLayer alpha.
examples.prompt: A download progress card: a bar filled to the progress, a percentage bubble that rides above the end of the bar, a row of level bars, and a caption that fades in as progress grows.
teaches: Pass an expression to a size modifier: {"fillMaxWidth": "@p"} fills that fraction of the parent, {"height": "10 + 54 * arrayGet(@eq, k)"} sets pixels
Move a component with {"offset": {"x": expr, "y": 0}}, clamping the expression so it stays inside its box
Fade a component with {"graphicsLayer": {"alpha": "0.2 + 0.8 * @p"}}
pitfalls: spacedBy parses an expression but the layouts keep it as a constant: "spacedBy": "@gap" writes a variable id that is used as a number (NaN), and the children lose their positions. Use constant spacing
Padding takes an expression only in its single-number form ({"padding": "@pad"}); the list and object forms are read as constants
fillMaxWidth's fraction is of the parent's width after its padding; the bubble's offset is in pixels, so it multiplies by the track width (328) itself

Inside a modifier, componentWidth() is the width of the component being modified (the 48 dp bubble), not of its parent: for a position along the parent, derive it from windowWidth() minus the padding, or a weight/fraction
Ten 22 dp bars with 8 dp gaps overflow a narrower host: give each bar weight 1 with widthIn [0, 30] and an end padding for the gap, so they shrink but never grow past the design

snippets.note: fillMaxWidth: "@p" — the bar fills 65 %
offset x = clamp(0, windowWidth() - 80, @p * (windowWidth() - 32) - 24): the bubble follows the bar end at any width (the bar spans the window minus the 16 dp padding each side)
height from an array element
graphicsLayer alpha 0.2 + 0.8 * @p

check.describe: The blue bar is filled to 65 % with a 65 % bubble centred over its end, ten purple bars of different heights below, and a dimmed caption. Resized, the bubble stays centred over the bar end (65 % of the live width), and the ten bars share the row (weight 1, at most 30 dp each with an 8 dp end padding as the gap): thinner at 234 wide, as at 360 when wider.

examples.name: text-formatting
examples.title: Number formatting flags
examples.summary: Eight numbers turned into text by textFromFloat flags and textMerge: thousands grouping, period-comma and underscore separators, negative parentheses, zero padding, mm:ss from seconds, a percent and whole-digit clipping.
examples.prompt: A reference card of number formats: $1,234.50, 1.234,50 €, 9_876_543, (42.50), 007, 07:05 from 425 seconds, 65 % and what happens when the whole digits are too few.
teaches: Add flags: AFTER 0 space/1 none/3 zero, PRE 0 space/4 none/12 zero, GROUPING 16 by 3, SEPARATOR 64 period-comma/128 space-comma/192 underscore, 256 negative in parentheses, 512 rounding
Build mm:ss from seconds: textMerge(textFromFloat(floor(@secs / 60), whole 2, flags 13), textMerge(":", textFromFloat(@secs % 60, whole 2, flags 13)))
Add a prefix or a unit with textMerge("$", number) or textMerge(number, " €"); nest textMerge for three parts
pitfalls: whole is the number of characters KEPT before the decimal point, separators included: 9,876,543 needs whole 9, and whole 3 prints 543
Without 512 (OPTIONS_ROUNDING) the decimals are cut, not rounded; with decimal 0 the C++ player ignores 512 too, so round() the value
A float holds about 7 significant digits: 1234567.89 is stored as 1234567.875; keep amounts below 2^24 or in cents
Inside a text value object decimal defaults to 3; set decimal 0 for whole numbers

A row of label and value with spaceBetween lets a long label push into the value when the host narrows: give the label column weight 1 and its texts maxLines 1 with ellipsis, so the value keeps its intrinsic width

snippets.note: textMerge("$", textFromFloat(@price, 7, 2, flags 23)) → $1,234.50
flags 87 = 64 PERIOD_COMMA + 16 BY3 + 7 → 1.234,50
flags 13 = 12 PAD_PRE_ZERO + 1 → 007
mm:ss from floor(s / 60) and s % 60, joined by textMerge

balance.meaning: account balance; negative shows in parentheses

big.meaning: a large count, grouped by thousands

code.meaning: a code shown zero-padded to 3 digits

secs.meaning: a duration in seconds, shown mm:ss

check.describe: Rows read $1,234.50, 1.234,50 €, 9_876_543, (42.50), 007, 07:05, 65% and 543. Resized, every formatted value stays whole at the end of its row: the label column takes what is left (weight 1) and ellipsizes on one line, so at 234 wide PERIOD_COMMA reads PERIOD_… beside 1.234,50 €; at 540 the rows spread out.

examples.name: text-ops
examples.title: String operations
examples.summary: A contact card built from three raw exported strings: textTransform capitalises the name, takes an upper-case initial and upper-cases the role, textMeasure sizes the role pill, textSubtext trims a preview and textLength counts its characters.
examples.prompt: A contact card from raw strings: "ada lovelace" shown as "Ada Lovelace" with an initial avatar, the role upper-cased in a pill that fits the text, and a 30-character preview of a message with its length.
teaches: Transform a string into a new text variable with textTransform {text, start, len, operation, varName}: 1 lower, 2 upper, 3 trim, 4 capitalise words, 5 capitalise first; len -1 runs to the end
Cut a substring with textSubtext {text, start, len, varName} and add an ellipsis with textMerge
Measure the rendered width with textMeasure (mode 0) after setting the paint's textSize, and size a pill with it: right = 122 + @roleW
Count characters with textLength {text, name} and print the count with textFromFloat
pitfalls: The JSON names for textTransform's operation are off by one in the reference parser: "uppercase" writes 1 (TEXT_TO_LOWERCASE), "lowercase" 2 (upper), "capitalize" 3 (trim). Write the number
textMeasure measures with the paint as it is at that point in the commands: set textSize first
textSubtext throws past the end of the string on Java (substring): keep start + len within the text, or use len -1
These operations are in the AndroidX profile: the header needs profiles 513 (the Java writer refuses opcode 199 without it)

A card drawn to x = 348 only fits the header width: draw it to componentWidth() - 12, and when the fixed-size text (a 21 px name, a 30-character preview) would no longer fit, scale the canvas down as a whole

snippets.note: textTransform operation 4: "ada lovelace" → "Ada Lovelace"
start 0, len 1, operation 2: the upper-case initial
textSubtext: the first 30 characters
textMeasure mode 0 → @roleW, the pill's width
textLength → @chars

its empty twin: 1 - clamp(0, 1, @rating - 2)

Snap to a page by rounding: page = round((2 * @w - @px) / @w)
Slide to the snapped page with an animated expression {"value": "@w * -@page", "anim": 0.35} and translate the strip of pages by it
Move the active dot with the same animated value (cx = 160 - @shift / 18), so the dot and the strip stay in step

snippets.note: the swipe, in px: dragging left lowers px; it starts at, and is capped by, 2 * @w (page 0), so the range follows the live width
page index: the nearest whole page, in page widths of the live componentWidth()
strip offset, animated over 0.35 s whenever page changes
page 2’s card: the strip is translated by the animated shift, then by one page width (@w) per card
the active dot, derived from the same animated shift: -20 - @shift / @w * 20 around the centred dots

check.describe: Starts on Today with the first dot lit; a 200 px swipe left lands on This week, with the second dot lit. Resized, a page is the live componentWidth() wide and the cards, labels and dots follow the box: at 234×200 a 140 px swipe (over half a page) lands on This week, at 540×260 a 300 px swipe does, with taller cards and the dots still at the bottom.

pitfalls: The Java JSON parser does not read touchSpec, so the notch stop modes (notchesEven and friends) cannot be configured from JSON, and on Android they index an empty spec; snap the displayed value with round() instead
Delta touch modes (0–5) move the value by the drag distance, so a leftward swipe lowers px; start at max (2 * @w = page 0) so swiping left can reach the later pages
Only the display snaps: the touch value keeps the fractional position, so the next swipe starts from where the last one ended rather than from the page boundary
A touchExpression expression element that is an infix formula is compiled separately; keep ["touchX()"] and scale afterwards if you want a release velocity

A pager that hard-codes the page width (360, 720) breaks as soon as the host is narrower or wider: read componentWidth() into a variable and use it for the page width, the touch range (defaultValue and max accept expressions) and the page index

onClick with four actions: tab = 2, show0 = 0, show1 = 0, show2 = 1
visibility: @show2

cross-axis centring; verticalArrangement centres the group on the main axis
spacedBy is a modifier, not a column property

Give each demo track the remaining width with weight 1 after a fixed-width label (a text with a width modifier)

spaceEvenly: four equal gaps, ends included
spaceAround: half-size gaps at the ends
