examples.title: Box alignment
examples.summary: Nine labelled tiles in one 300×300 box, each placed at one of the nine alignments from top-start to bottom-end.
examples.prompt: Place nine labelled tiles in one box, one at each corner, edge midpoint and the centre.
teaches: Overlap children by putting them in a box; each child is laid out on top of the previous one
Place a child at a corner, edge or centre with the box's horizontalAlignment (start/center/end) and verticalAlignment (top/center/bottom)
Give each child its own position by wrapping it in a fillMaxSize box with its own alignment
Make a fixed-width label tile from a single text: width, clip, background, vertical padding and textAlign center

snippets.note: top-start: a fillMaxSize box with horizontalAlignment start, verticalAlignment top
bottom-end: horizontalAlignment end, verticalAlignment bottom
the outer box stacks nine full-size layers
a tile as one text: fillMaxWidth 0.3 (never overlaps when narrow), clip, background, padding [0, 11], textAlign center

textAlign centres text only inside the text's own width: give the text a width (or fillMaxWidth), otherwise it wraps its content and there is nothing to centre in
Fixed-width tiles in a box overlap once the box is narrower than three of them: size them as a fraction of the width ({"fillMaxWidth": 0.3}) and give the labels maxLines 1 with an ellipsis

Let the last section take the remaining height with verticalWeight in a column (weight alone is horizontal)
Separate weighted children with fixed-size spacer boxes, which weights do account for

a column taking the rest of the height (verticalWeight 1), split 1:1 with verticalWeight
an 8 px spacer box between weighted children

weight is horizontal; in a column use verticalWeight

Cap a fillMaxWidth box with widthIn(min, max) so it stops growing on wide screens
Raise or cap an explicit width or height with widthIn / heightIn (width 40 + widthIn(100, 260) is 100 wide)

snippets.note: width 120 + height 28
size 40: one value for both axes
fillMaxWidth then widthIn [100, 260]: fills, but never wider than 260
width 40 + widthIn [100, 260]: the minimum wins, 100
height 80 + heightIn [16, 40]: clamped to 40

widthIn's minimum does not lift a fractional fillMaxWidth(0.3): at width 200 it stays 52.8 wide in the Java reference whatever the modifier order
An explicit size is still clamped by widthIn/heightIn: height 80 + heightIn(16, 40) is 40 tall, and width 40 + widthIn(100, 260) is 100 wide

examples.name: padding-offset-border
examples.title: Padding, offset and border
examples.summary: An outer card with a 2 dp rounded border and 16 dp padding, holding an inner card nudged by offset (8, 8) with rounded, clipped corners.
examples.prompt: A card with a 2 dp rounded outline and 16 dp padding containing a smaller rounded card nudged 8 dp right and down.
teaches: Draw a rounded outline with the border modifier {width, cornerRadius, color}, then inset the content with padding
Shift a child without changing the layout of its siblings with offset {x, y}
Round a card's corners with clip roundedRect before its background, so the background is clipped too

snippets.note: border 2 dp, corner 16, then padding 16
offset {x: 8, y: 8}
clip roundedRect 12 then background: the order matters

check.describe: The purple inner card starts 8 px right and below the outer card's padded corner (at 44, 44 instead of 36, 36), with rounded corners. Resized (200, 450 wide) the bordered frame fills the document inside its padding; the offset card keeps its size and its (8, 8) shift.

pitfalls: border cannot take an @colors reference: give it a literal colour
Modifier order is the paint order: clip must come before background or the background corners stay square; padding after background insets the content, not the background
offset moves only the drawing: the inner card keeps its layout slot, so it can overflow the outer padding (here it ends 8 dp further right and down)
border's cornerRadius only rounds with "shape": 2 (ROUNDED_RECTANGLE); the default shape 0 is a plain rectangle in Java, whatever the radius

examples.name: spacers
examples.title: Toolbar spacers
examples.summary: A toolbar row whose weighted spacer pushes two icon squares to the right end at any width.
examples.prompt: A toolbar with a title on the left and two action icons pushed to the right edge.
teaches: Push the following children to the end of a row with a spacer carrying weight 1
Put a fixed gap between two icons with a spacer of width 12
Centre the title and icons vertically in the toolbar with verticalAlignment center

snippets.note: spacer with weight 1 takes all the free width
a fixed 12 dp spacer between the icons

check.describe: The second icon is flush with the padded right edge: in the Java reference it sits at x=296 of a 328 px content row at width 360, and at x=176 of 208 at width 240. Resized (240, 540 wide) the weighted spacer absorbs the change: Inbox stays at the start and the two icons at the end.

pitfalls: A spacer with no modifiers gets weight 1 in the Java parser; a spacer with any modifier (such as width 12) gets no weight, so state the weight explicitly when you add one
Padding takes a list: [all], [horizontal, vertical] (here [16, 0]) or [start, top, end, bottom]; a three-value list writes no padding at all

examples.name: flow-chips
examples.title: Wrapping tag chips
examples.summary: Twelve rounded tag chips of different lengths in a flow that wraps them onto as many lines as the width needs.
examples.prompt: A wrapping row of rounded tag chips of different lengths that flows onto new lines.
teaches: Wrap children onto new lines when the row is full with a flow
Make a pill chip from one text: clip roundedRect, a background and inner padding [12, 6]
Space flow items with padding on a wrapper box (end and bottom 8 dp), since a flow ignores spacedBy

snippets.note: a fillMaxWidth flow of twelve chips
one chip: a padding [0, 0, 8, 8] gap box around a clipped, padded text pill

check.describe: Three lines of four chips at width 360; six lines at width 200 (C++ and TypeScript layouts agree). Resized: at 540 wide the chips fill two lines; at 240 wide they need five, more than 140 dp holds, so the root scrolls vertically (verticalScroll) instead of overflowing.

pitfalls: A flow ignores the spacedBy modifier (the Java reference and the C++ player both lay the chips edge to edge); give each item its own gap with padding on a wrapper

Do not fold the gap into the chip as a leading padding ([padding, clip, background, padding]): the Java player treats that first padding as a margin, but the C++ player paints the background over it, so keep the separate wrapper box
The Java layout reference measures text with a stub (100×10), so check line counts with the C++ or TypeScript layout, not java-layout.sh
A flow grows taller as its box narrows: in a fixed-height widget give the container a verticalScroll (or fewer items) or the last lines overflow the document

examples.name: fitbox-responsive
examples.title: Responsive fitBox
examples.summary: One weather card in a large, a medium and a small layout inside a fitBox, which shows the first one that fits the space it gets.
examples.prompt: A weather widget that shows a large, medium or small layout depending on how much space it gets.
teaches: Offer alternative layouts of the same content as fitBox children, ordered largest first: the first that fits without shrinking is shown and the others are gone
Give each alternative a fixed size (360×180, 230×130, 130×80) so the fit test has something to compare
Centre the chosen layout by letting the fitBox wrap it inside a centring box

snippets.note: fitBox with three children: large, medium, small
the smallest fallback, 130×80, with only the temperature

check.describe: Large card at 400×200, medium at 250×150, small at 150×100 (render_rc with width/height). The medium and small renders are the resize checks; wider than 400 the large card stays 360×180, centred.

pitfalls: Children are tried in order and the first that fits wins, so put the largest first; a fallback that is listed first hides the others
Give each alternative a fixed size: a fillMaxSize child takes whatever space it is given, so it always fits and the fallbacks after it never show

examples.name: vertical-scroll-list
examples.title: Vertical scrolling list
examples.summary: A 360×400 contact list of 12 rows (avatar, name, preview line) in a column that scrolls when dragged.
examples.prompt: A scrollable contact list with a round avatar, a name and a message preview on each row.
teaches: Make a column taller than the document scroll with the verticalScroll modifier
Bind the scroll position to a variable (resources.variables scroll: 0, verticalScroll "@scroll") so the player can drive and read it
Build a list row from a round avatar box and a two-line text column, spaced with spacedBy 12

snippets.note: the scroll position variable, starting at 0
verticalScroll bound to @scroll
one 64 dp row: avatar, name and preview, spacedBy 12

check.describe: Before the drag rows 1–6 are visible; after dragging (180,350)→(180,50) the list is scrolled to its end, showing rows 7–12. Resized (300×560, 540×300) the rows stretch to the width and the list scrolls in whatever height it gets; the same swipe moves it by the same 300 dp.

A list only scrolls if its content is taller than the viewport: here 12 × 64 dp rows in a 400 dp document

examples.name: horizontal-carousel
examples.title: Horizontal carousel
examples.summary: Five 200 dp destination cards in a row that scrolls sideways when dragged.
examples.prompt: A horizontally swipeable carousel of destination cards.
teaches: Let a row wider than its container scroll sideways with horizontalScroll bound to a variable
Space fixed-width cards with a spacedBy 12 modifier (fine here: no child has a weight)
Anchor a card's text to its bottom with verticalArrangement bottom

snippets.note: horizontalScroll bound to @scroll, after the padding
one card: width 200, fillMaxHeight, rounded, bottom-aligned text
the scroll position variable

check.describe: At rest cards 1 and 2 show; after dragging from x=330 to x=30 cards 3 and 4 are in view. Resized: at 540 wide more of the cards show after the same swipe; at 160 high the cards fill the shorter height, their captions staying at the bottom.

pitfalls: Bind the scroll position to a variable: the C++ player does not scroll a constant position such as {"horizontalScroll": 0}
For snapping pages instead of free scrolling see INT-06 (pager)

examples.name: visibility
examples.title: Gone versus invisible
examples.summary: Two A-B-C lists side by side: on the left B is gone and its space collapses, on the right B is invisible and leaves a gap.
examples.prompt: Three items where the middle one has visibility gone, then invisible (two variants side by side).
teaches: Hide a component with the visibility modifier, which reads an integer variable: 0 gone, 1 visible, 2 invisible
Collapse a hidden item's space with gone (0), or keep its space with invisible (2)
Declare each visibility as an exported integer in resources ("@leftB") so the host can show or hide the item

snippets.note: exported integers leftB = 0 (gone) and rightB = 2 (invisible)
B with visibility @leftB (0, gone): C moves up
B with visibility @rightB (2, invisible): a gap stays

leftB.meaning: visibility of the left B: 0 gone, 1 visible, 2 invisible

rightB.meaning: visibility of the right B: 0 gone, 1 visible, 2 invisible

check.describe: Left: A then C directly below it. Right: A, an empty slot the size of B, then C (Java reference: right C 44 px lower than left C). Setting rightB to 1 shows B again. Resized (240, 540 wide) the two panels share the width; at 240 the "B invisible (2)" caption wraps, and the gap B leaves is still there.

pitfalls: visibility takes an integer variable id, not a boolean or a string: a literal such as {"visibility": 2} is read as variable id 2, not the value invisible
Unexported integers used only by visibility are reported as dead_code by the audit; exporting them (the host's switch) avoids it
Invisible keeps B's space and its spacedBy gap; gone removes both

examples.name: collapsible-row
examples.title: Collapsible app bar (priorities)
examples.summary: An Inbox app bar shown at five widths: a collapsibleRow drops its children by collapsiblePriority as space runs out (the unread chip first, then share, then search), keeps the unprioritized title and overflow menu longest, and a weighted spacer keeps the icons pushed to the end at every width.
examples.prompt: An app bar (title "Inbox", a "12 new" chip, search, share and an overflow menu) that drops its least important items as it narrows: the chip first, then share, then search; the title and the overflow menu stay. Show it at 328, 240, 200, 152 and 112 dp.
teaches: Let a collapsibleRow decide what fits: children are kept in priority order (highest first) and dropped from the lowest priority up once the next one no longer fits
Rank children with collapsiblePriority {orientation: horizontal, priority: N}; leave the must-stay ones (title, overflow menu) without a priority, which counts as the highest
Push the actions to the end with an unprioritized weighted spacer: it takes only the space left over and never causes a drop
Size the container, not the collapsibleRow, when its children include a weight: give the row fillMaxWidth inside a box of the width you want
pitfalls: Unprioritized children all tie at the top and keep document order among themselves: at 112 dp the title (first) stays and the overflow menu (last) goes

The fit test adds up the children's widths only, not spacedBy: with spacedBy 10 a 225 dp row keeps 220 dp of children and overflows by 20 dp. Build gaps into the children's own widths (as the 76 dp title box does) instead
Priorities compare by the integer part of their difference, so values less than 1 apart tie and 2, 2.5, 3 is not a consistent order (at 250 dp Java keeps 3 and 2 and drops 2.5): use whole numbers
Dropping stops at the first child that does not fit: a lower-priority child that is narrow enough to fit is dropped too, so give similar-sized items adjacent priorities

Don't give the weighted spacer a priority: it is then ranked and dropped like any other child as soon as space is short (at 200 dp a priority-0 spacer went while 40 dp were still free), and the remaining items re-centre instead of staying at the ends
A child with a weight makes a row or collapsibleRow ignore its own width modifier and fill its parent (Java, matched by both players): wrap it in a box of the width you want

A nested collapsibleRow is measured against the width left after its earlier siblings in document order, not after the higher-priority ones, so its own drops can interleave oddly with the parent's (an inner label kept while a higher-priority sibling goes, then the reverse a few dp narrower)
A demo of fixed widths overflows a narrower host if one of them is as wide as the header's content area: make the widest one fillMaxWidth so it becomes the live, resizing case

snippets.note: the whole bar: collapsibleRow with title, chip, spacer and three icons
the chip's collapsiblePriority 1: the first to go
search, priority 3: the last action to go
unprioritized weighted spacer: takes the leftover width only

check.describe: Five bars: the first is full width (328 dp at 360) and shows everything; 240 dp drops the "12 new" chip; 200 dp also drops share; 152 dp also drops search (title and overflow menu left); 112 dp keeps only the title. The icons stay right-aligned in every bar. Verified against Java (java-layout.sh 360 400): the same children are gone and the C++ and TS x/width match it. Resized: the full-width bar is the live one — at 300 wide (268 dp) it has already dropped the chip, at 540 it shows everything with the icons at the far end; the four fixed-width bars below are unchanged.

examples.name: collapsible-column
examples.title: Collapsible weather column
examples.summary: A narrow weather widget at four heights: a collapsibleColumn keeps city and temperature (no priority), then the icon, high/low and condition by vertical collapsiblePriority, and three tied forecast rows that drop from the bottom up.
examples.prompt: A tall, narrow weather widget (city, sun icon, temperature, condition, high/low, three hourly forecast rows) that sheds content as it gets shorter: the forecast rows go first from the bottom, then the condition, then high/low, then the icon; city and temperature always stay. Show it at 256, 208, 164 and 100 dp.
teaches: Stack a widget's content in a collapsibleColumn so rows that don't fit the height are dropped instead of clipped
Rank the rows with collapsiblePriority {orientation: vertical, priority: N}; leave the rows that must stay (city, temperature) without one
Give repeated rows the same priority: tied children keep document order, so the forecast drops from the bottom row up
Put the padding and background on a wrapping box and give the collapsibleColumn fillMaxSize, so fillMaxWidth rows stay inside the padding
pitfalls: The priority's orientation must match the container: a horizontal collapsiblePriority on a collapsibleColumn child is ignored and the child counts as unprioritized (kept first)

A collapsibleColumn's own padding is not applied to its children's fill width: a fillMaxWidth row inside a padded collapsibleColumn comes out as wide as the column and offset by -padding (Java, matched by both players). Pad a wrapping box instead
Rows are kept in priority order, not document order: at 164 dp high/low (priority 3) stays while the condition above it (priority 2) goes, and the remaining rows close up

Dropping stops at the first row that does not fit: every row after it in priority order goes too, even one small enough for the space left (a 10 dp priority-1 row is dropped under a 40 dp priority-2 row that did not fit). Give similar-sized rows adjacent priorities
Give the rows fixed heights (here 20–48 dp boxes) when the result has to be predictable: a text's height depends on the font and the player

A row of fixed-width demo cards is wider than a narrow host: give the row a horizontalScroll (bound to a variable — a literal position leaves its touch expression unused, which the audit reports as dead code)

snippets.note: the collapsibleColumn with its eight rows, inside the padded card box
condition, vertical priority 2: goes before high/low (3) and the icon (4)
a forecast row, priority 1: the three tie and drop bottom-up

check.describe: Four cards: the first fills the height (256 dp at 300) and shows everything; 208 dp keeps one forecast row; 164 dp keeps city, icon, temperature and high/low (the condition and forecast are gone); 100 dp keeps city and temperature only. Verified against Java (java-layout.sh 360 300): the same rows are gone and the C++ and TS bounds match it. Resized: the full-height card is the live one — at 360×200 it (and the taller fixed cards, squeezed to the row) keep city, icon and temperature; at 360×400 it shows everything with room to spare; at 240 wide the row scrolls horizontally (horizontalScroll) rather than cutting the last card.

examples.name: state-layout
examples.title: Three-state status card (StateLayout)
examples.summary: A photo-backup card with three layouts (up to date, backing up, paused) held by a stateLayout and picked by an exported integer: each state's root taps to the next state, and components paired by animationSpec animationId (the card, its header row, the badge, the title) morph between them while the rest enter and exit.
examples.prompt: A photo backup status card with three states chosen by an integer the host can set: a compact "Up to date" row, an expanded "Backing up" card with a progress bar and Pause/Details buttons, and a red "Paused, no Wi-Fi" card with Retry. Tapping the card goes to the next state, and the card animates its size and the header between them.
teaches: Hold one layout per state as the children of a stateLayout and pick one with indexId, an integer variable (here an exported integer the host can set to 0, 1 or 2)
Advance the state from each state's root: an onClick with valueIntegerChange to the next index (1, 2, then back to 0), with semantics describing what the tap does
Pair the parts that exist in every state with the same animationSpec animationId (card 200, header row 203, badge 201, title 202) so they morph in size and position; unpaired parts enter and exit
Size each state for its own content (72, 148 and 128 dp): only the current state is measured, so the stateLayout resizes with it
pitfalls: An onClick on the stateLayout itself is not dispatched by Java: put one on every state root
Pair components with animationSpec animationId: the `id` modifier (component id) does not pair them across states. The state roots need no component ids at all; give them distinct ones if you set any

Keep paired components at the same depth in every state (here each state's header is one row with animationId 203): during the transition the previous state's direct children that the new state lacks are painted as exiting, so a badge that is a direct child in one state and nested in another was painted twice (a stray green corner in the C++ player)
Keep a paired text the same size in every state: its bounds morph, and a text that grows is cut short mid-transition ("Photo" instead of "Photo backup")

The index is read at paint time and the new state is laid out on the next frame, so capture a change at least a frame later. An index with no matching child is ignored: with state 3 the card stays on the state it had (state 0 at start) in Java and C++, so keep the exported range 0..2

snippets.note: stateLayout with indexId @state and three state roots
the exported integer that selects the state (0 up to date, 1 backing up, 2 paused)
state 0's tap: valueIntegerChange state = 1
the badge's animationSpec animationId 201, shared with the badges of the other states
the stateLayout's own animationSpec: 350 ms STANDARD resize

state.meaning: which layout is shown: 0 up to date, 1 backing up, 2 paused (no Wi-Fi)

check.describe: A tap on the compact card at 0.1 s, captured settled at 0.9 s: the expanded "Backing up" card with progress bar and Pause/Details. Mid-transition (0.2 s) the card is half grown with the badge already blue. variables {"state": 2} shows the red Paused card with Retry; a second tap from state 1 goes there and a third back to the compact row. Verified against Java (java-layout.sh 360 220 --click 180 52 --settle, then --click 180 100): the stateLayout is 72, 148, 128 then 72 dp high, and C++ and TS match. Resized (240×220, 540×300) the card fills the width; at 240 the status line wraps to two lines and the progress bar follows the card's width.

examples.name: baseline-align
examples.title: Number and unit on one baseline
examples.summary: A run summary (8.42 km, 42:10 min, 5′01″ /km) twice: with the row's default centring the small units float at mid-height, with alignByBaseline on the number and the unit they share the number's text baseline.
examples.prompt: A run summary card with three stats (distance 8.42 km, time 42:10 min, pace 5′01″ /km), each a big number followed by a small unit that sits on the number's baseline, with a label below. Show the same card with default centring above it for comparison.
teaches: Put alignByBaseline on every text of a row to line their first baselines up, whatever their font sizes
Keep a unit next to its number in its own small row, and lay the stats out in a collapsibleRow with spaceBetween so a narrow card drops the last stat instead of cutting it
pitfalls: Put alignByBaseline on every child of the row: once one child has it, a child without it is placed with its top on the shared baseline (Java RowLayout gives it an align offset of 0), so a unit without it drops below the number
With alignByBaseline the row's verticalAlignment moves the aligned group as a whole; it no longer centres each child on its own

Player status (2026-10-29): the C++ player aligns baselines; the TS player ignores alignByBaseline and puts the units at the top of the row. The Java layout harness (MockRemoteContext) measures every text 100×10, so it can't check baselines

Weighted stat columns (weight 1 each) never shrink below their content: when the card narrows the numbers overlap and the last unit is cut. Size stats to their content in a collapsibleRow (spaceBetween) so the last one drops out; a weighted child is never dropped by a collapsibleRow

snippets.note: 8.42 (26 sp) and km (13 sp), both with alignByBaseline
the unit's alignByBaseline, before its 3 dp left padding
the same pair with verticalAlignment center, for comparison

check.describe: Top card: km, min and /km float at mid-height of the big numbers. Bottom card: their bottoms sit on the numbers' baseline (C++: the 13 sp unit 15.1 dp below the row top instead of 8.8). Resized: at 540 wide the three stats spread to the card's edges; at 240 (and already at 300) the collapsibleRow drops Pace rather than overlapping or cutting the numbers, and the captions end in an ellipsis.

examples.name: pattern-counter
examples.title: A template with local state
examples.summary: One CounterButton template used three times; each instance keeps its own tap count in a template-local variable.
examples.prompt: Make three buttons (Save, Share, Delete) from one reusable button template, each showing how many times it was tapped.
teaches: Define a component once with definePattern: parameters (label, color) and locals (taps)
Give each instance its own state: a local variable, incremented by its own onClick
Call a template like a built-in component: {"CounterButton": {"label": "Save", ...}}

snippets.note: the template: parameters label and color, local taps
onClick: taps = taps + 1 (per instance)
a call, by parameter name

check.describe: Tapping Save twice shows 2 under Save only; Share and Delete stay at 0. Resized, the buttons share the row: at 221 wide all three shrink to about 56 dp (labels still fit) and Save counts on its own; at 510 they stay 96 dp, at the start of the row.

pitfalls: List per-instance state in `locals`: it gets a pattern-local id that each inflation renames, which is what keeps Save's count separate from Share's
Inside the template, parameters are plain @name references everywhere, including semantics ("contentDescription": "@label") and modifier values ("background": "@color")
textFromFloat keeps only `whole` integer digits and pads with leading spaces: whole 3 with flags 4 shows 0..999 centred, where whole 2 would show 100 taps as "00"

Fixed 96 dp buttons overflow a host narrower than the header (221 dp cuts off Delete): give the template box weight 1 with widthIn [0, 96] so the three calls shrink to share the row but never grow past 96, and put 12 dp spacer boxes between the calls, since weights ignore spacedBy

examples.name: month-grid
examples.title: Month calendar from nested loops
examples.summary: A month calendar drawn by a week loop around a weekday loop: each cell's day number comes from the two indices and the month's first weekday, and step masks hide days outside the month, dim weekends and circle today.
examples.prompt: Draw a month calendar for October 2026 (starts on a Thursday, 31 days) with Monday-first weekday initials, weekends dimmed and today, the 29th, circled.
teaches: Nest two loops (week 0..6, weekday 0..7) and turn the two indices into one value: day = week * 7 + wd + 1 - @firstWeekday
Name a per-iteration value with a variable command inside the loop body and reuse it in later commands of the same iteration
Hide, dim or show an item per iteration without a branch: a 0/1 step mask as paint alpha (inside the month, weekends) or as a radius (today's circle)
Drive a loop's content from exported variables, so the same document renders any month
pitfalls: step(a, b) is 1 only when a > b (strict): test day >= 1 as step(@day, 0.5) and day <= 31 as step(31.5, @day)

Avoid conditionalOperations inside a loop for anything that reads the loop index through an expression: a block updates all its commands' inputs before running them, so an expression computed in the block is one iteration late, and a value computed before the block may not refresh at all (C++). Masks keep it right
There is no break: a loop always runs from..until. Make the bounds cover the worst case (6 weeks) and mask the cells you do not want

Derive the cell pitch from componentWidth()/componentHeight() once (two variable commands before the loops) instead of literal 41 × 38 cells: the loop body reads @cw and @rh every iteration, and the weekday letters step along with translate(@cw), which costs no new expression

This grid is fixed to October 2026 to keep the loop lesson small (rc-inspect flags it: hardcoded_date). For 'this month' or 'today', compute the month, the weekday of the 1st, the day count and today from the clock, as TIM-10 does; never paste them.

snippets.note: outer loop over weeks, inner loop over weekdays
day number from both indices and @firstWeekday
inMonth: 1 for 1 <= day <= monthDays, else 0
paint alpha = inMonth, dimmed on weekdays 5 and 6

today.meaning: day of the month to circle (0 for none)

check.describe: October 2026: 1 under Thursday, 31 under Saturday, Saturday and Sunday columns dimmed, 29 in a blue circle; no numbers before the 1st or after the 31st. Resized (small 200×220, large 450×450) the grid spreads over the canvas: cells are cw = (componentWidth() - 13) / 7 wide and rh = (componentHeight() - 72) / 6 high, and today's circle is 0.42 × the smaller of the two.

examples.name: agenda-pairs
examples.title: Loop over data in pairs
examples.summary: Today's meetings stored as one flat array of start/end hours; a loop with step 2 and until = arrayLength draws one bar per pair, labels its duration and dims the ones already over, over an hour grid drawn by a second stepped loop.
examples.prompt: Show today's meetings (9:00–10:30, 11:00–12:00, 13:30–14:30, 15:00–16:45) as bars on an 8 to 18 h timeline with hour labels, each bar labelled with its length, a red now line at 14:00 and finished meetings dimmed.
teaches: Store records as consecutive values in one floatArrays (start, end, start, end …) and walk them with loop step 2: arrayGet(@meetings, i) and arrayGet(@meetings, i + 1)
Bound a loop by the data, not a constant: until = arrayLength(@meetings), so adding a pair adds a bar
Use a loop's from/until/step for an axis: hours 8..18 every 2 with the index itself as the label
Derive per-item state from the item: alpha 1 - 0.6 * step(@now, end) dims a meeting once it is over
pitfalls: The loop index counts array slots, not records: with step 2 the k-th record is at i = 2k, so a row position written i * 15 moves 30 px per record
until is exclusive and is compared with the index (i < until): until = arrayLength(@meetings) stops at the last pair; until 19 with from 8 step 2 still reaches 18
A loop has no break or filter: hide the items you do not want with a mask (alpha, size), or prepare the array so it only holds what to draw
Put the axis scale in one variable from componentWidth() (px) rather than a literal 31 px per hour in every expression: the timeline then fits any width

snippets.note: loop i from 0 until arrayLength(@meetings) step 2: one bar per (start, end) pair
dim when the end is before @now
hour grid: loop h from 8 until 19 step 2, index printed as the label
the records, flattened

check.describe: Four bars on four rows: 1.5 h and 1.0 h dimmed (before 14:00), 1.0 h (13:30–14:30, crossing the red now line) and 1.75 h bright; hour labels 8 to 18; "4 meetings" top right. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the 8–18 h axis spans the canvas: one hour is px = (componentWidth() - 50) / 10, read by the grid, the now line and every bar, and the count stays at the right edge.

examples.name: loop-bounds
examples.title: Loops with variable bounds
examples.summary: A water-intake tracker whose glasses come from two loops bounded by host variables: filled glasses from 0 to min(drunk, goal), empty outlines from drunk to goal; an empty range simply draws nothing.
examples.prompt: A water tracker widget: a row of glasses for a daily goal of 8, the 5 already drunk filled blue and the rest as outlines, "5 of 8 glasses", a progress bar and "3 to go".
teaches: Repeat a drawing a variable number of times: loop until "min(@drunk, @goal)" (an expression bound is re-read whenever the variable changes)
Start a second loop where the first stopped (from "@drunk" until "@goal") to draw the remainder in another style
Rely on empty ranges instead of if: when from >= until the loop body never runs (0 drunk: no filled glasses; goal reached: no outlines)
pitfalls: Clamp a bound that can exceed the space you drew for: min(@drunk, @goal) keeps a ninth glass off the row
Set the paint before the loop when every iteration shares it; a paint inside the body is re-applied on every iteration
The index is a float: from "@drunk" = 4.5 gives 4.5, 5.5, …; floor the bound if the variable can be fractional

Space loop items by a pitch derived from the width and the item count, g = (componentWidth() - 40) / @goal, rather than a literal 40: a fixed pitch overflows a narrow host and leaves a gap on a wide one

snippets.note: filled glasses: loop i from 0 until min(@drunk, @goal)
outlines: loop i from @drunk until @goal

goal.meaning: daily goal in glasses (8 fit the row)

check.describe: Five filled glasses then three outlines, "5 of 8 glasses", the bar at 62 %, "3 to go". drunk 0 gives eight outlines; drunk 9 gives eight filled glasses and "0 to go". Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the row of glasses spans the canvas: the pitch is g = (componentWidth() - 40) / @goal and each glass is gw = min(28, 0.7 g) wide, so the goal's glasses always fill the row; the bar and the count follow the width.

examples.name: switch-cases
examples.title: Switch on a state code, with a default
examples.summary: A weather card that switches on an integer condition code: one eq block per case, a shared cloud drawn once for the range of cases 1–3, and a default case written as the two complementary blocks lt 0 and gt 3; rem commands label the cases in the document.
examples.prompt: A current-weather card that shows a sun, cloud, rain or snow icon with its name and one line of advice, chosen from a condition code 0–3 (here 2, rain), and a "No data" state for any other code.
teaches: Write a switch as one conditionalOperations eq block per case value: only the matching block runs
Share drawing between several cases with a range block (ge 1 containing le 3) placed before the per-case blocks, like a fallthrough
Write the default case as the complement of all cases: here lt 0 plus gt 3, two blocks with the same content (there is no else and no or)
Label sections of a long command list with rem: a comment the document carries and players ignore
pitfalls: The Java parser knows only gt, ge, lt, le and eq: any other name, ne included (a json2rc extension), becomes 0, which is EQ, so a ne block silently runs when the values are equal, the opposite of what was meant
eq compares floats exactly: switch on whole-number codes, never on a computed fraction
A gap in the codes needs its own default block: with codes 0, 1 and 3, the default is lt 0, eq 2 and gt 3
Paint state carries across blocks: set colour and size at the top of every case, or a case inherits whatever the previous one set
A canvas laid out at fixed coordinates needs a fit rule: here one variable and a translate + scale at the top keep it centred and on screen at any size, without touching the cases

snippets.note: case 2: eq @condition 2, rain drops and text
range block for cases 1-3: the shared cloud
default, first half: lt 0
default, second half: gt 3
rem: a comment kept in the document

condition.meaning: 0 clear, 1 cloudy, 2 rain, 3 snow; anything else is no data

check.describe: condition 2: a cloud with three blue rain streaks, "Rain", "Take an umbrella.". 0 gives the yellow sun with eight rays, 1 the cloud alone, 3 the cloud with snow dots, -1 or 4 a grey "?" and "No data". Resized, the drawing is centred vertically (translate componentHeight() / 2 - 85) and shrinks below 300 dp wide (scale min(1, componentWidth() / 300)) so the longest line still fits: at 240 it is drawn at 0.8.

examples.name: pattern-list
examples.title: A list from a template and a data list
examples.summary: A favourites list whose five rows are one ContactRow template (definePattern) inflated by patternForEach over a list of names; each row derives its avatar initial from its name with textSubtext, and the name list is hoisted out of the layout with a global section.
examples.prompt: A favourites contact list (Ada Lovelace, Barbara Liskov, Claude Shannon, Edsger Dijkstra, Grace Hopper): each row has a round avatar with the initial, the name and a chevron, built from one row definition repeated over the list of names.
teaches: Define a row once with definePattern (parameter who) and repeat it for every item of a data list with patternForEach {collection, localItem, children}
Pass the current item to the template by name: {"ContactRow": {"who": "@name"}}, where name is the patternForEach localItem
Derive per-row values inside the template from its parameter (textSubtext of @who gives the avatar initial), so the data list stays one string per row
Hoist the data list out of the layout with a global section in a canvas: it is written before the root, like a resource
pitfalls: addDataList cannot be named in the Java parser (U4), so collection is the list's numeric id: 2097194 (0x20002A) for the first array of a document. A floatArrays resource or another list before it moves that id
addDataList is a canvas command, not a component: it needs a canvas around it (here a 0-size one, its command wrapped in global)
A pattern name must not match a built-in component case-insensitively: a template called Row fails with "Cannot override pre-existing component"
patternForEach gives one id per item; a row needing several fields needs them derived from that one string (or one template call per row instead of a data list)

snippets.note: patternForEach over list 2097194, item bound to name, one ContactRow call per item
the ContactRow template: parameter who
textSubtext(@who, 0, 1): the initial
the names list, hoisted before the root

check.describe: Five rows under FAVOURITES, in list order, each with a blue initial avatar (A, B, C, E, G), the full name and a grey chevron. Resized (narrow 220, wide 540) every inflated row fills the width with the chevron at the right edge; a long name ellipsizes on one line.

examples.name: pattern-slot
examples.title: A template with a content slot
examples.summary: One Panel template (rounded surface, muted title) used twice with different content: the template marks where content goes with patternArgument, and each call passes its own components in a patternBlock for that parameter.
examples.prompt: Two dashboard panels in the same style: STORAGE with "41.6 of 64 GB used" and a usage bar, and RECENT DOWNLOADS with two files and their sizes; define the panel frame once and give each its own content.
teaches: Leave a hole in a template with {"patternArgument": {"parameterIndex": 1}}: parameter 1 (content) is a slot, not a value
Fill the slot at the call: the call's children hold {"patternBlock": {"parameterIndex": 1, "children": [...]}}, any components at all
Mix value parameters and slots: title is passed by name ("title": "STORAGE"), content as a block
pitfalls: parameterIndex counts the template's parameters from 0 (title is 0, content 1); the slot parameter still has to be declared in parameters
The block lands where patternArgument sits, inside the template's container: it is laid out by that column, so it is stacked, not overlaid
A slot that is not given renders nothing, with no error

snippets.note: the slot: patternArgument parameterIndex 1
the call's content: patternBlock parameterIndex 1
Panel template, parameters title and content

check.describe: Two identical rounded panels: STORAGE with 41.6 large, "of 64 GB used" and a 65 % blue bar; RECENT DOWNLOADS with two file names and their muted details. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) both panels fill the width and the storage bar is drawn from componentWidth(), so it stays at 65 % of its panel.

examples.name: pattern-vs-component
examples.title: Format template vs library component
examples.summary: The same key/value spec row built twice: four SpecRow calls of a definePattern template that the player inflates, and four calls of the KeyValueRow library component that json2rc expands into plain components before writing. They look the same; the template costs about 48 B per extra row, the expanded component about 200 B (KeyValueRow v3, whose key ellipsizes in a weighted box).
examples.prompt: A phone spec card (Display 6.1 in OLED, Chip A18, Storage 256 GB, Battery 3,561 mAh) built once with a definePattern row template and once with the KeyValueRow library component, to compare them.
teaches: Choose definePattern when the same row repeats: the body is stored once in the .rc and each call is a pattern inflation with its argument ids (measured here: 840 B for 1 row, 1078 B for 6, about 48 B per extra row)

Choose a library component (KeyValueRow) for richer options (slots, $if, theme tokens) resolved at conversion: json2rc expands each call into plain components, so every call costs its full body (788 B for 1 row, 1641 B for 6, about 171 B per row)
Re-theme library components by defining their colours (surface, muted, onSurface) in resources.colors; a template reads the same named colours through @colors
pitfalls: A text inside a template measures as one component for every instance (U7): two intrinsic-width texts in a row collide, clipped to one instance's width. Give template texts a weight or fixed width (here both texts take weight 1, the value right-aligned)
The break-even is about two rows: with one call the template's definition (about 52 B) is pure overhead
The Java parser only sees the expanded document: a library component call is a json2rc feature, and doc.expanded.json is what is byte-checked; definePattern is in the format and every parser reads it

snippets.note: SpecRow template: key and value, both texts weighted
a template call: {"SpecRow": {key, value}}
the library call: {"KeyValueRow": {key, value}}, expanded at conversion

check.describe: Two cards with the same four rows, keys muted on the left and values right-aligned; the top card's label says definePattern, the bottom one KeyValueRow. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) both cards fill the width, keys stay left and values right in both builds, and a caption too long for the card ellipsizes.

examples.name: referenced-include
examples.title: Record once, include anywhere
examples.summary: A verified badge (a small canvas with a circle and a tick) recorded once with referencedOperations and placed after three names with include; the document is 900 B against 1163 B with the badge written out three times.
examples.prompt: A reviewers list (Margaret Hamilton, Ken Thompson, Linus Torvalds, Frances Allen) where every name but Linus's has the same small blue verified tick after it; draw the tick once and reuse it.
teaches: Record a fragment once with {"referencedOperations": {"name": "Verified", "children": [...]}}: it is stored, not shown
Place it wherever it is needed with {"include": {"value": "@Verified"}}: the player splices the recorded components in at that spot
Prefer it over copying for anything drawn more than once without parameters (icons, dividers, logos); use definePattern when the copies differ
pitfalls: Declare referencedOperations at the top level of a root array, next to definePattern: there it is recorded in the first pass. Declared inside a column it is also drawn where it is declared, and in the C++ player its includes then lose components
A recording has no parameters: every include is identical. For a label or colour that changes, use a template (STR-06, RU-05)
The included canvas keeps its own size modifiers; give the canvas a fixed size, since it has no intrinsic size

snippets.note: the recording: one 18 dp canvas with the tick
include @Verified after a name

check.describe: Four names under REVIEWERS; Margaret Hamilton, Ken Thompson and Frances Allen each followed by the same blue circle with a white tick, Linus Torvalds without. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the list keeps its left edge and each tick follows its name; the rows are as wide as their content, so nothing depends on the header width.

examples.name: modifier-macro
examples.title: Shared styles as modifier macros
examples.summary: Two style macros, a definePattern whose only child is a modifier list: ButtonStyle (height, pill clip, a fill colour parameter, padding) styles three buttons, TagStyle (no parameters) two tags; each box applies one with an includeMacro modifier, then adds its own ripple and semantics.
examples.prompt: A row of three pill buttons (Save in blue, Share in purple, Delete in red) and two small grey tags (draft, 3 attachments) below, with the button and tag styles each defined once and shared.
teaches: Define a style as a template holding only a modifier list: {"definePattern": {"name": "ButtonStyle", "parameters": ["fill"], "children": [{"modifier": {"modifiers": [...]}}]}}
Apply it with a modifier, among the component's own: {"includeMacro": {"pattern": "ButtonStyle", "arguments": ["#FF4DA3FF"]}}, then ripple and semantics after it
Parameterise only what varies (the fill colour) and keep the rest of the look in one place
pitfalls: arguments is positional and always required, even for a style with no parameters ("arguments": [])
The macro's modifiers are inserted where includeMacro sits in the list, so order still matters: padding in the macro, after its background, pads the content inside the pill

Small savings: about 73 B here (1113 B against 1186 B with the modifiers written out, measured on the one-row version). A macro is mainly for consistency; byte savings grow with the size of the shared list and the number of uses

A row of intrinsic-width buttons squeezes the last one to a sliver on a narrow host: a flow wraps it to the next line instead (a flow ignores spacedBy, so the gaps are spacer boxes, here 54 dp tall to space the lines too)

snippets.note: ButtonStyle: a template whose body is a modifier list, fill as a parameter
includeMacro ButtonStyle with the blue fill
TagStyle: a style with no parameters

check.describe: Three 44 dp pill buttons (blue Save with dark text, purple Share, red Delete) and below them two small rounded grey tags. Resized: the buttons sit in a flow, so on a narrow host (240×190) Delete wraps to a second line instead of being squeezed; the 10×54 spacers keep a gap between the lines. Below about 300 dp wide the widget needs the extra height.

examples.name: global-section
examples.title: Shared definitions in a global section
examples.summary: A steps widget whose shared numbers (goal, gap) sit in a global section at the top of the root, with a rem comment, and whose ring progress is computed inside the canvas but wrapped in a global command, so the converter moves it before the root where every component can read it.
examples.prompt: A daily steps widget: a green progress ring with the percentage in the middle, and beside it "Steps today", 7,420 and "2,580 to go" against a 10,000 goal; keep the goal and spacing as shared constants.
teaches: Group document-wide definitions in {"global": {"children": [...]}} at the top of a root array: variables (and rem comments) defined once, read anywhere as @goal, @gap

Hoist a value computed where it is drawn: {"global": {"commands": [...]}} inside a canvas moves those commands before the root, so @progress is computed before any layout and is visible to every component
Use the same token in a modifier and a drawing: @gap pads the row and sizes the spacer box
pitfalls: A global section's children must be definitions (variable, definePattern, referencedOperations, createFloatFunction, …); anything else in it is silently skipped

Do not use a vtype color variable as a paint colour: Java writes its id as a literal ARGB (transparent) and json2rc writes opaque black. Colours for paints and text belong in resources.colors, used as @colors.accent
global moves bytes, it does not copy them: the hoisted commands leave the canvas, so anything they define is computed once for the document, not per paint of that canvas
A fixed 140 dp ring leaves the numbers no room on a narrow host: give the ring canvas a weight and draw it from componentWidth()/componentHeight(), capped at its design size

snippets.note: global section: rem plus the goal and gap tokens
global command in a canvas: progress hoisted before the root
rem: a comment stored in the document
colours as named colour resources

check.describe: A green ring three quarters full with 74% inside; beside it "Steps today", 7,420 and green "2,580 to go". Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the ring and the numbers share the row by weight: the ring is centred in its half, its radius min(56, min(componentWidth(), componentHeight()) / 2 - 14) shrinks on a small host, and the percentage's text size follows the radius.

examples.name: float-function
examples.title: A drawing helper as a float function
examples.summary: A heart-rate sparkline whose lowest, highest and latest readings are marked by one helper, pin(i, size, sx, sy), defined once with createFloatFunction: it looks up the reading, draws a ringed dot and the value label, and is called three times with callFloatFunction.
examples.prompt: A heart-rate line chart for today (14 readings) with the lowest (55), highest (95) and latest (64) readings marked with a red dot and their value, the latest one larger; draw the marker with one reusable helper.
teaches: Define a helper once with {"createFloatFunction": {"name": "pin", "params": ["i", "size", "sx", "sy"], "commands": [...]}}: the params are plain names in the body's expressions
Call it with {"callFloatFunction": {"id": "@pin", "args": [6, 3, "@px", "@py"]}}: one call per marker, the latest one bigger (args [13, 5, …])
Read outer data in the body (arrayGet(@bpm, i)) so a call passes only what differs (which point, how big) plus the chart's scale (@px, @py, from componentWidth()/componentHeight())
Let a function return its result by drawing: the body's draw commands run at each call site, in order with the surrounding commands
pitfalls: A variable command inside the body is a new local binding, not an assignment: a function cannot set an outer variable (the Java parser restores the variables after the body), so return values by drawing, or compute them as expressions at the call site
Paint changes made in the body stay in effect after the call: set colours inside the function, and again after it if later commands need another one
Arguments are positional: args must list a value for every param, in the params order
An expression argument ("arrayLength(@bpm) - 1") converts and runs, but rc-inspect's audit then reports it as dead_code: the audit does not yet count function arguments as uses

Pass size-dependent values to the function as arguments (here the scale @px, @py): a body that reads componentWidth(), or a variable computed from it, breaks the C++ player's later drawing in the same canvas (the line and the right-aligned label vanish); TS draws it right

snippets.note: pin(i, size, sx, sy): ring, dot and value label at reading i, placed with the scale passed in
call for the latest reading: args [13, 5, @px, @py]
the line: one segment per pair of readings, px apart

check.describe: A red line over 14 readings; red dots with dark rings and labels at 55 (third point), 95 (seventh) and a larger one at 64 (last). The C++ and TS players render it the same. Resized (narrow 240, large 540×260) the line spans the canvas: px = (componentWidth() - 48) / 13 per reading and py = (componentHeight() - 70) / 60 per bpm, passed to pin as its sx, sy arguments, so the markers stay on the line.

examples.name: digital-clock
examples.title: Digital clock
examples.summary: HH:MM:SS in large digits: hour, minute and second read from the clock and zero-padded to two digits.
examples.prompt: Make a digital clock that shows the current time as HH:MM:SS in large digits.
teaches: Read the clock: timeInHr() for the hour, timeInMin() % 60 for the minute, timeInSec() % 60 for the second
Zero-pad each field to two digits with textFromFloat whole 2, decimal 0, flags 12 (PAD_PRE_ZERO)
Lay the fields and colon separators out in a row

snippets.note: hours: textFromFloat(timeInHr(), 2 digits, zero padded)
minutes: timeInMin() % 60 (timeInMin is minutes since midnight)
seconds: timeInSec() % 60 (timeInSec is seconds within the hour)

check.describe: At 10:10:05 it reads 10:10:05; at 09:05:07 it reads 09:05:07 with leading zeros. Resized, the time stays centred in the box (a layout box with centred alignment); it needs about 220 dp of width at fontSize 56.

pitfalls: timeInMin() is minutes since midnight and timeInSec() seconds within the hour, so both need % 60 to give a clock field
Without flags 12 (PAD_PRE_ZERO) textFromFloat pads with spaces, so 9 shows as " 9" rather than 09
timeInHr() is the 24-hour hour (0–23); a 12-hour clock needs (timeInHr() + 11) % 12 + 1
A clock field needs decimal 0: inside a text value object decimal defaults to 3

examples.name: analog-clock
examples.title: Analog clock
examples.summary: Hour, minute and second hands driven by the clock, over twelve ticks drawn with a loop.
examples.prompt: Draw a round analog clock face with twelve ticks and hour, minute and second hands showing the current time.
teaches: Rotate a hand around the centre with save + rotate(angle, pivotX, pivotY)
Drive the angles from the clock: (timeInMin() % 720) * 0.5 for hours, (timeInMin() % 60) * 6 for minutes, (timeInSec() % 60) * 6 for seconds
Draw evenly spaced ticks with a loop and a rotation by index (i * 30)
Set the shared stroke style and round cap once, and only colour and width per hand
Fit a drawing authored at the header size to any box: a variable s = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H), a translate by half the extra space and a scale by s about the design's centre

snippets.note: hour hand: (timeInMin() % 720) * 0.5 degrees
second hand: (timeInSec() % 60) * 6
twelve ticks: loop i, save, rotate i * 30 about the centre

Keep float precision by subtracting day and second-of-day parts separately: (targetDay - dayOfYear()) * 86400 + (targetSec - secondOfDay)
Name the remaining seconds once in resources.variables and split it into hours, minutes and seconds with floor and %

snippets.note: seconds to 2026-10-29 12:24:12 UTC (day 302, second 44652), clamped at 0
hours: floor(@remaining / 3600), zero padded
minutes: floor(@remaining / 60) % 60

check.describe: At 2026-10-29 10:10:05 UTC (epoch ms 1793268605000) it reads 02:14:07 in any time zone; at the launch instant and after, 00:00:00. Resized, the column stays centred both ways and keeps its three lines.

epochSecond() converts with json2rc but the Java parser does not know it; build absolute time from dayOfYear(), timeInMin(), timeInSec() and offsetToUtc() instead
A float has 24 bits of mantissa: seconds-since-Jan-1 (~3e7) lose whole seconds, so subtract the target's day and second-of-day separately; the formula only works within one calendar year
Hours are floor(@remaining / 3600) with no % 24: past 99 hours whole 2 drops the leading digit, so add a days field (or whole 3) for a longer countdown

examples.name: month-calendar
examples.title: Evergreen month calendar
examples.summary: A month calendar computed entirely from the clock: the month name and year, the weekday of the 1st, the number of days (28 to 31, leap years included) and today's circle all come from date expressions, so the same document is right every month without being regenerated.
examples.prompt: Make a month calendar widget for the current month: the month name and year as a title, Monday-first weekday initials, a 6×7 grid of day numbers with weekends dimmed and today circled. It must stay correct next month and next year without regenerating the document.
teaches: Weekday of the 1st from today alone: fw = (weekDay() - dayOfMonth() + 35) % 7 (0 = Monday; the + 35 keeps the left side positive, so % never sees a negative number)

Days in the month without a table: 30 + (m + floor(m / 8)) % 2 for every month but February (31/30 alternate and flip at August), minus (2 - leap) when m = 2, with leap = [y%4=0] - [y%100=0] + [y%400=0] and each [x=0] written 1 - min(1, x)

Month name without a data list: textSubtext of a 12 × 9-character table at (calendarMonth() - 1) * 9, then textTransform operation 3 (trim) to drop the padding; textMerge it with textFromFloat(year())
One cell definition for all 42 cells: a week loop around a weekday loop, day = week * 7 + wd + 1 - @fw; step masks hide the days outside 1..@nd and circle the one equal to dayOfMonth()
Theme colours (@colors.surface, onSurface, muted, primary, onPrimary) with "componentTheme": "auto" at the top give light, dark and (built with componentTheme mono) monochrome from one document

snippets.note: weekday of the 1st: (weekDay() - dayOfMonth() + 35) % 7
days in the month from calendarMonth() and the leap-year flag
Gregorian leap year with % and 1 - min(1, x) as 'is zero'
month name: a 9-character slot of a padded table, picked by calendarMonth()
the 6 × 7 grid: one cell body inside a week loop and a weekday loop
inMonth: 1 for 1 <= day <= @nd, else 0
isToday: 1 when day = dayOfMonth()

check.describe: Canonical 2026-10-30: October 2026, the 1st under Thursday, 31 days, 30 circled. feb-leap (2028-02-14): February 2028, 1st on Tuesday, 29 days, 14 (a Monday) circled. feb-common (2027-02-01): February 2027 fills exactly four rows, 1st on Monday circled, 28 days. jan-sat (2022-01-31): January 2022 starts on Saturday, 31 days spill into a sixth row, 31 (Monday) circled. sep-sun (2024-09-30): September 2024 starts on Sunday, 30 days, 30 alone on the sixth row. Weekend columns are dimmed; no number appears before the 1st or after the last day. light and mono re-colour the same layout. Resized (small 200×210, wide 460×300) the cells are (componentWidth() - 16) / 7 by (componentHeight() - 80) / 6 and the day text scales with them (9 to 20).

pitfalls: Hard-coding the month: a literal "October 2026", a firstWeekday of 3 or a monthDays of 31 makes a document that is wrong in two days. Derive all three from weekDay(), dayOfMonth(), calendarMonth() and year()

weekDay() is 1 = Monday … 7 = Sunday and dayOfMonth() starts at 1: the 1st's offset is (weekDay() - dayOfMonth()) mod 7, and a negative left side must be lifted (+ 35) before %, which keeps the sign of the dividend

Day count: (m + floor(m / 8)) % 2 gives 31 for Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec; forgetting the August flip (m % 2 alone) makes August 30 days and September 31. February is 28 + leap, and leap needs the 100 and 400 rules (2100 is not leap, 2000 was)
Writing 31 (or 42) cell copies by hand: one loop body with a computed day number and step masks is a fraction of the size and covers every month shape (4, 5 or 6 rows)
There is no break: loop over the worst case (6 weeks × 7 days) and hide the extra cells with a 0/1 alpha mask; step(a, b) is strict, so 1 <= day <= nd is step(day, 0.5) * step(nd + 0.5, day)
Don't build the month name with addDataList + textLookup: the Java parser drops the list id (U4). A fixed-width textSubtext table plus a trim converts identically everywhere
Today's text sits on the primary circle: draw the number twice, onSurface with alpha inMonth * (1 - isToday) and onPrimary with alpha isToday, rather than one colour that is unreadable on the circle

Date fields alone never schedule a repaint (only continuousSec, timeInSec, timeInMin and wakeIn do, EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U6): this document is idle and turns the page at the host's next redraw. If it must flip at midnight on its own, also read timeInMin() somewhere (a repaint a minute)

examples.name: moon-phase-calendar
examples.title: Moon phase calendar
examples.summary: Tonight's moon drawn large with its phase name, the percentage lit, its age and the days to the next full and new moon, over a calendar of the month with each day's moon and the day of each principal phase labelled. Everything comes from the clock through a small lunar ephemeris (mean elongation plus five periodic terms), so the document stays right every month.
examples.prompt: create an app with the phases of the moon for this month
teaches: The moon is the MoonPhase library component, called with a phase computed in the document ({"MoonPhase": {"phase": "@f", "size": 112}}); the 42 day moons are the same geometry drawn once inside the calendar's week x weekday loop, not 42 canvases

Days since 2000-01-01 00:00 UTC at the start of today: 365 * (year() - 2000) + floor((year() - 1997) / 4) + dayOfYear() - 1 - offsetToUtc() / 86400. offsetToUtc() makes the days local, so a phase lands on the user's calendar day

The lunation count L(t) = 0.8104301 + 0.033863192 t (the mean elongation over 2π) plus five sines (equation of centre, evection, variation, the Sun's anomaly, the second centre term): every principal phase from 2015 to 2045 within about 40 minutes of Meeus' full algorithm, on the right day for 99.5% of them

A day holds a principal phase when floor(4 L) changes across it: ev = floor(4 L(k + 1)) - floor(4 L(k)), and floor(4 L(k + 1)) % 4 says which (0 new, 1 first quarter, 2 full, 3 last quarter). The phase name and the grid labels use the same rule, so they never disagree

Days to the next full (or new) moon: the target lunation N = floor(L - 0.5) + 1.5, a first guess at the mean rate, then two Newton steps t -= (L(t) - N) * 29.53; counted from the start of today, so on the day itself it reads "today" until midnight
The phase name is a 15-character slot of a padded table (textSubtext) trimmed with textTransform 3; the today / tomorrow / in N days variants are three texts switched by 0/1 paint alpha

snippets.note: days since 2000-01-01 UTC at the start of today, from year() and dayOfYear()
offsetToUtc() turns the local midnight into UTC days
the lunation count at the start of today, first half: mean elongation and the two largest terms (a Java expression holds at most 32 entries, so the series is split in two)
second Newton step towards the next full moon
phase-name index: a principal phase today, else the in-between name
tonight's moon: the MoonPhase component at phase @f, 112 dp
phase name from a padded table, trimmed
the 6 x 7 month grid: one cell body in a week loop and a weekday loop
ev: 1 on the day a principal phase happens
the day's moon: lit half, then the terminator ellipses, as MoonPhase draws it

check.describe: Renders pin offsetToUtc() to 0 (system variable 10), so days are UTC days and the result doesn't depend on the build machine's time zone. Canonical 2026-10-30 12:00: a waning gibbous moon lit on the left, "Waning Gibbous", 76% illuminated, age 19.6 days, full moon in 25 days (Nov 24), new moon in 10 days (Nov 9); October 2026 starts on Thursday, Last Q under the 3rd, New under the 10th, 1st Q under the 18th, Full under the 26th, 30 outlined. nov-full (2026-11-24): "Full Moon", full moon today, new moon in 15 days; November starts on Sunday (six rows): Last Q 1, New 9, 1st Q 17, Full 24. nov-new-eve (2026-11-08): "Waning Crescent", new moon tomorrow, full moon in 16 days. pacific (2026-11-08, offset -8 h): the 07:02 UTC new moon is 23:02 on the 8th locally, so "New Moon", new moon today, New under the 8th and Last Q under the 30th (Dec 1 06:09 UTC). light and mono re-colour the same layout (mono: white lit parts, black shade, grey rims). small (300 x 520) and wide (480 x 640): the cells are componentWidth() / 7 by (componentHeight() - 52) / 6 and the moons and day numbers scale with the smaller of the two.

pitfalls: Don't draw the moons as text glyphs (🌑 🌓 🌕 ◐): they depend on the device's fonts, can't follow the theme, and show 8 phases at best. Draw them (MoonPhase, or its geometry inside a loop)

Don't paste a canvas per day with the phase typed in: 31 or 42 copies are large, one wrong copy goes unnoticed, and the document is wrong next month. One loop body with the day computed from the loop indices draws every month

Don't hard-code the month, its first weekday, its length or the phase dates ("Full moon Oct 26"): derive the month from calendarMonth(), weekDay(), dayOfMonth() and year() (TIM-10), and the phases from an ephemeris of the clock

Local time vs UTC: the date functions are local, the ephemeris is in UTC days. Subtract offsetToUtc() / 86400, or an evening full moon west of Greenwich (Oct 26 04:11 UTC is Oct 25 in California) lands a day late. For renders, pin system variable 10 (offsetToUtc) so they don't depend on the machine's time zone

The mean lunation alone (t / 29.53 days) puts phases up to 19 hours off. The LLM version's two-term correction (the new/full-moon coefficients) still missed the quarters by up to 6 hours, because evection adds about 0.22 days there: 7.5% of principal phases from 2015 to 2045 landed on the wrong day (Nov 1 2026's last quarter on Nov 2). The five-term series here puts 0.5% of them on the wrong day, each within an hour of midnight

Days to the next full moon from the mean rate alone can be a day off (the true rate varies by about 15%): refine with two Newton steps, and count from the start of today, not from now, so the day of the full moon reads "today" and not "in 29 days" after the moment has passed

A float expression holds at most 32 entries in Java (Limits.MAX_EXPRESSION_SIZE; the parser and the player both throw "to long"), and json2rc, C++ and TS don't check it: the five-term series written as one expression converts and renders, then fails on Android. Split it (la0 = mean + two terms, la = la0 + three terms) and pass each time as a single variable, not "(@d0 + 1)" repeated six times
In a column, the child that takes the remaining height needs verticalWeight; ["fillMaxWidth", {"weight": 1}] there gives a canvas 0 wide and the grid vanishes
Date functions alone never schedule a repaint: the illumination reads timeInMin(), which repaints once a minute and turns the page at midnight

examples.title: Text overflow and ellipsis

Give the text a fixed width (a width modifier on the text itself) so it has something to overflow

maxLines 1, overflow start_ellipsis
maxLines 1, overflow middle_ellipsis

step(x, edge) is x > edge, and clamp takes (min, max, value)

the same icon in the three styles and filled
a status icon with its accessibility label

The name must exist: an unknown name fails with the closest matches; search by meaning with find kind "icons" (tags such as 'battery', 'signal', 'weather')

components.name: moon-phase
components.title: Moon phase
components.prompt: Draw the moon at any phase of its cycle, from new through full and back, without glyphs or images; show the eight principal phases captioned, and one bound to a variable.

Draw in a 100-unit box and scale it to size once; with a literal phase every expression folds to a number, so a static moon costs no expressions

snippets.note: 0, a new moon: the 100-unit drawing scaled to 48 dp, a rim and an unlit disc
0.125, a waxing crescent: the right half lit, then a shaded ellipse over it
0.375, a waxing gibbous moon: the right half and a lit ellipse
bound to the exported variable phase: the terminator follows cos(2π·@phase)

phase.meaning: lunation fraction 0..1 of the large moon

check.describe: Two rows of four 48 dp moons, captioned with the phase and its name: 0 new (an empty disc inside its rim), 0.125 a thin crescent lit on the right, 0.25 the right half lit, 0.375 gibbous lit on the right, 0.5 full, 0.625 gibbous lit on the left, 0.75 the left half lit, 0.875 a crescent on the left. Below, a 72 dp moon bound to phase 0.3 (a waxing gibbous moon, 65% lit). Dark: amber on slate; light: the theme's darker amber on pale grey; mono and mono inverted: the lit part in onSurface, the rest background inside a grey ring. At 260 dp the columns close up and at 480 dp they spread; the moons keep their size.

components.summary: The moon at a phase of its cycle (0 new, 0.25 first quarter, 0.5 full, 0.75 last quarter), drawn from circles, a half-disc and an elliptical terminator in a square canvas.
pitfalls: Don't draw a moon as a text glyph (🌒 ◐ ☾): it depends on the device's fonts, can't take theme colours or a size, and shows eight phases at best. Call MoonPhase with the phase computed in the document
Waxing is lit on the right (phase < 0.5) and waning on the left, as seen from the northern hemisphere; for the southern hemisphere mirror it (a scale of -1 around the centre) or pass 1 - phase
phase is the fraction of the lunation, not the fraction lit: the lit fraction is (1 - cos(2π · phase)) / 2, so a quarter moon (0.25) is half lit, and 0.125 is about 15% lit

The terminator is an ellipse of half-width r · |cos(2π · phase)|, in the shade colour for a crescent (cos > 0) and in the lit colour for a gibbous moon (cos < 0). Each is drawn with a width of max(0, ±cos), so the other one has zero width: no paint alpha to switch and reset
At exactly new moon the lit half isn't drawn (its sweep is 180 · step(0.9999, cos)): the shaded ellipse covers it, but the half-disc's antialiased edge would still leave a lit hairline on the limb
The edge ring is a disc 1 dp larger drawn first, not a stroke drawn last: a stroke over the disc dulls the lit limb

Mono ignores lit, shade and rim: the lit part is onSurface and the rest background inside a 1.5 dp outline ring, so the phase reads as shape. On black (mono) that is a white full moon; in mono inverted (e-ink) the lit part is the ink, so a full moon is a black disc, the reverse of a printed almanac's ● new / ○ full: label the phases there
